topics.name: Interactive media and the user experience

dotPoints.description: Investigate how interactive media and the user experience (UX) is used to communicate information to an audience

prompts.question: Outline two features of interactive media that help a website communicate information to its audience.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional council launches a website with flood-warning maps that residents can zoom and filter, river-level graphs and short instructional videos. Many residents check the site on a phone during storms, so the council needs the information to be quick to understand.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines TWO features of interactive media that help the council's website communicate information to residents
2 marks: Outlines ONE feature and how it helps residents understand information OR Identifies TWO features of interactive media
1 mark: Identifies ONE feature of interactive media for the website
markerNotes: Name two different features, such as zooming, filtering or a clear layout, and say what each does for the reader.
Each feature needs a link to communicating information; a feature with no effect on understanding earns no credit.
A brief outline of one or two sentences per feature is enough for this question.
commonStudentErrors: Listing parts of a website, such as the logo or the colours, without saying how they communicate information.
Describing interactive media in general terms, such as saying it is popular with young people, rather than naming a feature.
Giving the same feature twice in different words, such as 'zoom' and 'magnify'.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interactive media lets residents zoom and filter the flood map, so they can find the streets that matter to them. Clear labels and a consistent layout also support the user experience (UX), helping the audience read the warning quickly on a small phone screen. Together these features communicate information more effectively than a static notice.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines two features, the zoomable and filterable flood map and clear labels with a consistent layout, each linked to helping residents read the warning, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Residents can zoom and filter the flood map, which helps them find their street. The website also has videos, which make it more interesting to visit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one feature, zooming and filtering the flood map, and how it helps residents, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain a second feature, such as clear labels, and how it helps residents understand the warning.

sampleAnswers.answer: A flood map that residents can zoom into.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one feature, a flood map that residents can zoom into, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, outline how the feature helps residents understand the warning.

prompts.question: Explain how the user experience (UX) of a touch-screen exhibit affects how well school students understand the information it is designed to communicate.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional museum installs a touch-screen exhibit about the history of its local river for school groups. The exhibit has a main menu, large buttons, short videos and a timed quiz at the end, and the museum wants students to leave understanding how the river shaped the town.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains how specific UX features of the exhibit affect students' understanding, with clear cause and effect
4 marks: Explains how one UX feature of the exhibit affects understanding, with a clear link to the content
3 marks: Explains one way the UX affects understanding, with some link to the exhibit
2 marks: Identifies a UX feature of the exhibit and states that it affects students
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Show the chain from a design feature to what the student does or understands; that cause and effect separates a strong answer from a description.
Use the exhibit in the scenario, such as the menu or the button feedback, rather than discussing user experience in general.
Name the information being communicated so the marker can see that the design choices serve the content.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the exhibit's features, such as its screens and colours, without saying how they affect understanding.
Stating that good UX makes the exhibit 'better' without a cause-and-effect explanation.
Discussing user experience in general terms that could apply to any website, rather than the touch-screen exhibit.

sampleAnswers.answer: The user experience (UX) of the exhibit determines whether students can follow the interactive media content. When the main menu is simple and the buttons are large, students can move straight to the river history and focus on its message. Clear feedback, such as a highlighted button when it is pressed, tells students that their choice has registered, which reduces confusion. Consistent icons and a clear back button also mean students do not have to relearn the controls at each station. If the navigation is cluttered, students spend their time working out the controls instead of reading, so they understand the content less well. Good UX therefore keeps the audience focused on the message, which is how the exhibit can communicate information effectively to its audience.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains specific UX features of the exhibit, such as the simple menu and clear feedback, with cause and effect for students, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A simple menu helps students use the exhibit, so they can read the river history. Good design makes the exhibit easier to use for everyone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains one UX feature, the simple menu, with a link to reading the content, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, explain the cause and effect of the menu on students' understanding of the content.

sampleAnswers.answer: The exhibit is easy to use, so students learn more.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information that the exhibit is easy to use, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify a UX feature of the exhibit and say it affects students.

dotPoints.description: Investigate social, ethical and legal issues when developing and implementing interactive media systems

prompts.question: Outline one social, one ethical and one legal issue a developer must consider when implementing the quiz app.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a developer is building an interactive quiz app for high school students. The app records each student's answers, shows a class leaderboard with students' names, and sends weekly progress reports to parents through an online platform.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines one social, one ethical and one legal issue, each explained and linked to the quiz app's features
3 marks: Outlines all three categories, with explanation linked to the app for at least TWO of them
2 marks: Outlines TWO of the three categories OR Identifies all three categories
1 mark: Identifies ONE relevant social, ethical or legal issue
markerNotes: Give one social, one ethical and one legal issue as separate categories, since ethics concerns what is fair and legal concerns what the law requires.
Link each issue to the quiz app, such as the leaderboard or the parent reports, rather than naming a general concern.
A legal issue should refer to a real obligation, such as the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), explained in terms of its effect on the app.
commonStudentErrors: Naming two issues in the same category, such as two social issues, and leaving the ethical or legal part blank.
Treating legal compliance and ethical responsibility as the same point, so one issue is counted twice.
Giving a single word such as 'privacy' with no explanation of how the app creates the issue.

sampleAnswers.answer: A social issue is that the class leaderboard may embarrass students who score poorly, so the developer should consider showing results privately. An ethical issue is that the app records every answer, so the developer should collect only the data needed for learning and be open with students and parents about what is kept. A legal issue is that the developer must consider the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), which governs how personal information such as student results is collected, used and disclosed in progress reports. Each consideration shapes how the interactive media systems are designed and who they serve.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines all three categories, each explained and linked to the quiz app's features and users, which meets the 4-mark row. The Privacy Act reference is specific and applied to the app.

sampleAnswers.answer: The class leaderboard may embarrass students who score poorly, which is a social issue. The app also records answers, so the developer should think about what data is kept, an ethical issue.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines a social and an ethical issue, each linked to the app, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, outline a legal issue and link all three categories to the app's features.

sampleAnswers.answer: Privacy is a concern when students use the app.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one relevant issue, privacy, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, outline a social or ethical issue and link it to the app.

prompts.question: Discuss the trade-off a developer faces when an interactive media system stores detailed student data to personalise feedback.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the developer of the quiz app wants the system to store each student's pattern of errors so that it can recommend targeted practice. Some teachers support the feature, while some parents and students are concerned about who could see the stored data and how it would be used.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses the trade-off between personalised feedback and the risks of storing student data, reaching a reasoned conclusion
5 marks: Discusses both sides of the trade-off, with relevant social, ethical and legal points
4 marks: Discusses the benefits and at least one concern of storing student data, with reference to the app
3 marks: Identifies relevant issues of storing student data, with some link to the app
2 marks: Identifies a benefit OR a concern of storing student data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about student data
markerNotes: Weigh the benefit against the risk for the same students, rather than listing benefits and risks in separate paragraphs.
Refer to the quiz app and the developer's choice to store error patterns, so the discussion stays on this system.
A reasoned conclusion, such as support with consent and an opt-out, is what lifts a discussion into the top band.
Answers could include: privacy of stored student data; fairness of feedback; consent and an opt-out; who can see the stored data
commonStudentErrors: Listing social, ethical and legal issues as separate points with no link between them or to the trade-off.
Saying that collecting data is simply 'bad' without weighing the benefit to students.
Treating a legal obligation as an ethical choice, or the reverse, without explaining the difference.

sampleAnswers.answer: The developer's case for storing error patterns is that personalised feedback can help students improve faster, and teachers may welcome a system that targets practice. However, the student data is personal and could reveal weaknesses that students would prefer to keep private, which is a social concern if classmates or parents can see it. Ethically, the developer must be transparent about what is stored and must not use the data for purposes students did not expect. Legally, privacy law requires the developer to limit collection to what is needed, keep the data secure and use it only for the purpose for which it was collected. The trade-off is justified only if students and parents are informed and can opt out, with informed consent given before any data is stored. On balance, the interactive media system can improve learning without eroding trust, but only under these conditions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses the trade-off, weighing personalised feedback against social, ethical and legal issues of the stored data, and reaches a conditional conclusion, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Storing error patterns could help students improve, but the student data is personal and could be seen by others. The developer must be transparent about what is stored and collect only what is needed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses a benefit and a concern of storing error patterns, with reference to the app, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, discuss both sides with social, ethical and legal points.

sampleAnswers.answer: Personalised feedback helps students, but the stored data is private, so the developer should be careful.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a benefit and a concern, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, identify the relevant issues of storing student data and link them to the app.

dotPoints.description: Research the evolution of interactive media (prevalence of blogs, online video and digital radio; privacy issues and the use of intellectual property, including Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP))

prompts.question: Describe how the growing prevalence of blogs and online video has changed the ways a local history society can share its research.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a local history society has completed a study of its town's early buildings. Its members are deciding whether to publish the findings as a blog, as a short online video series or as a segment on a community digital radio station.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes TWO distinct ways blogs and online video change how the society shares its research, each linked to the scenario
3 marks: Describes TWO ways blogs or online video change sharing, with one linked to the society's research
2 marks: Describes ONE way blogs, online video or digital radio changes how research is shared
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about blogs, online video or digital radio
markerNotes: Describe the change itself, such as readers commenting on blog posts or viewers seeing buildings on screen, rather than just naming the format.
Link each change to the society's research, for example the buildings it studied.
Two distinct ways earn credit; the same idea repeated in two wordings earns one mark.
commonStudentErrors: Naming blogs, online video and digital radio without describing how they have changed the way research is shared.
Writing that the internet is 'good' or 'modern' without describing a specific change.
Describing one format in detail and ignoring the others in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: The growing prevalence of blogs means the society can publish its research as written articles that readers can comment on, which turns the publication into interactive media that invites discussion. Online video lets the society show the buildings visually, so viewers can see architectural details that a written report cannot convey. A community digital radio segment offers a spoken option that reaches listeners who may not read online. Each format reaches a different audience, so the society's choice depends on which community members it wants its research to reach.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two distinct changes, commenting on blog articles and seeing the buildings on video, each linked to the society's research, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Blogs let the society post research online, so more people can read it. This is easier than printing a report.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one way blogs change sharing, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe a second way, such as online video, and link one of the two ways to the society's research.

sampleAnswers.answer: Online video is popular, so the society could use it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information that online video is popular, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe one way online video changes how research is shared.

prompts.question: Assess the privacy and intellectual property risks, including ICIP, of publishing the society's material as an online video series.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the society's research includes recorded interviews with long-time residents, a family's private photograph collection, and an Aboriginal place name and oral stories about the river, shared with the society by local Traditional Owners. The society wants to publish all of this material as a free online video series.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the privacy, intellectual property and ICIP risks, weighing their seriousness and reaching a justified judgement about the video series
5 marks: Assesses at least TWO risk areas with relevant detail, including ICIP
4 marks: Discusses TWO relevant risks with reasons linked to the scenario
3 marks: Identifies relevant privacy or copyright risks, with some link to the video series
2 marks: Identifies ONE relevant risk of publishing the material
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about privacy or copyright
markerNotes: Weigh the risks against each other and say which matters most, with reasons; a list of risks alone stays in the middle band.
Recognise that owning a recording does not settle whether cultural knowledge can be shared, which is the core of ICIP.
End with a judgement on whether and under what conditions the series should be published.
Answers could include: privacy of interviewees and families in the photographs; copyright in photographs and recordings; ICIP for the place name and oral stories
commonStudentErrors: Treating privacy, intellectual property and ICIP as the same issue, or using them as synonyms.
Stating that ICIP is just copyright, which misses the cultural rights of the Traditional Owners.
Listing risks without a judgement about whether the society should publish.

sampleAnswers.answer: Privacy is the first risk. The recorded interviews reveal personal information about residents, and the family photographs may show people who never agreed to appear in a public online video. The society should obtain informed consent from each interviewee and check that the family permits publication. Intellectual property is a second risk: the photographs and interview recordings belong to their creators, so the society needs permission before it reproduces them. The most serious risk concerns Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP). The place name and oral stories are cultural knowledge held by the Traditional Owners, so publishing them without their consent could breach ICIP principles even though the society holds the recording. The society should consult the Traditional Owners and remove or defer that material. Overall, the society should not publish the online video series until consent and cultural approval are secured, since the risks to people and to cultural knowledge outweigh the benefit of an early release.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses privacy, intellectual property and ICIP risks, identifies ICIP as the most serious, and gives a conditional judgement on publication, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Privacy is a risk because interviewees and families in the photographs may not have agreed to publication. Intellectual property also matters, since the society needs permission to publish photographs it did not take.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses privacy and intellectual property risks with reasons linked to the scenario, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, assess ICIP in detail, given the place name and oral stories in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Publishing the interviews online could breach residents' privacy, so the society should be careful.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one relevant privacy risk with little development, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, identify relevant risks and link them to the video series.

dotPoints.description: Describe the contribution of interactive media systems to a range of enterprises (how simulation, gamification and augmented reality (AR) support online training and learning; how streaming services, gaming and virtual reality (VR) improve access to entertainment; how specialist apps support delivery tracking, advertising and communication)

prompts.question: Demonstrate, with a specific example, how a specialist app can support delivery tracking for a regional courier company.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional courier company wants to improve communication with its customers. It is considering a delivery-tracking app that customers can open on their phones, and an online training module for new drivers.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Demonstrates one clear contribution of a specialist app to delivery tracking, with a specific example from the courier scenario
2 marks: Demonstrates a relevant contribution of a specialist app, with a general example
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of a specialist app
markerNotes: Name the specific contribution, such as tracking or alerts, and show how it changes something for the business or the customer.
The specific example is what earns the top mark; a general statement that apps are useful earns less.
Keep the example tied to the courier company's situation in the scenario.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a specialist app without saying what it contributes to the enterprise.
Describing an app that does not fit the question, such as a game or a streaming service, rather than a delivery-tracking app.
Giving a general example, such as 'apps make things easier', instead of a specific feature for the courier.

sampleAnswers.answer: Specialist apps are interactive media systems that support enterprises. For example, the courier's app sends each customer a notification when the driver is two stops away, which supports delivery tracking and communication between the business and its customers. Customers can prepare for the drop-off, so fewer parcels are missed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Demonstrates one clear contribution, customer notifications when the driver is two stops away, with a specific example from the courier, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A tracking app shows customers where their parcel is, which helps with communication.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Demonstrates a relevant contribution with a general example, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, give a specific example that uses the courier's app, such as customer notifications.

sampleAnswers.answer: Specialist apps can send alerts to customers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a relevant feature, alerts to customers, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, explain how the alerts contribute to delivery tracking.

prompts.question: Analyse how simulation, gamification and augmented reality could support the online training of the courier company's new drivers, and weigh one limitation of the online program.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional courier company trains many new drivers each year. Training is currently a classroom course, and many drivers find the safe lifting and loading rules hard to remember. The company is considering an online program that includes a simulated loading dock, points and badges for completed modules, and an augmented reality overlay of safety prompts on real parcels.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how each of simulation, gamification and augmented reality supports driver learning, and weighs a limitation
5 marks: Analyses at least TWO of the tools with clear links to driver learning
4 marks: Analyses TWO tools with some links to training outcomes
3 marks: Describes the tools and their general purpose for the courier's online training
2 marks: Identifies ONE tool and a benefit of online training
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about gamification or simulation for training
markerNotes: Analyse by linking each tool to a learning benefit, such as repeated practice or retention, rather than describing what each tool is.
Use the courier scenario, such as safe lifting or loading routines, to ground the analysis.
A limitation, such as cost or the need for accurate simulations, shows the balanced thinking the top band requires.
commonStudentErrors: Defining simulation, gamification and augmented reality without explaining how each supports training.
Claiming the tools will 'definitely' make drivers safer, with no reasoning about how they work.
Writing about streaming or virtual reality entertainment, which is outside this training scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Simulation supports online training by letting new drivers practise loading and delivery routines in a virtual depot without risk to staff or parcels. Each practice run can be repeated until the driver is confident, which builds skill more effectively than a single classroom session. Gamification adds motivation: points and badges for completed modules encourage drivers to finish the program and revisit the safety rules, reinforcing learning over time. Augmented reality extends this by overlaying safety prompts onto a real parcel through a phone camera, so a driver sees the correct lifting method at the moment it is needed. Together, these tools make training interactive and memorable. The main limitation is cost, because the company must produce accurate simulations and test them on the devices drivers actually use, so the benefit depends on careful development. The simulation can also record each driver's errors, so trainers can target coaching at the rules a driver finds hardest.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses all three tools by linking each to driver learning and retention, and weighs the cost limitation, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Simulation lets drivers practise routines safely before real deliveries. Gamification with points and badges can motivate drivers to complete their online training, which supports learning, though the benefit may fade.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses two tools, simulation and gamification, with some links to training outcomes, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, analyse augmented reality as well, with a clear link to driver learning.

sampleAnswers.answer: Gamification with badges makes the training more fun for drivers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one tool, gamification, and a benefit, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe what the tools do for the courier's online training.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate the performance requirements of hardware for specific interactive media projects

prompts.question: Calculate the storage needed for this uncompressed video, in megabytes (MB), where 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes. Show your working and give the answer to one decimal place.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a studio is producing a 10-second product demonstration for a museum display. The video is 1280 pixels wide by 720 pixels high, uses 24-bit colour (3 bytes per pixel) and plays at 30 frames per second. The studio's first draft is uncompressed, so every frame is stored in full.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Calculates the bytes for each frame and the total for ten seconds at 30 frames per second, stating 829.4 MB with working shown
2 marks: Calculates the bytes needed for one frame correctly and attempts the total for the full clip
1 mark: Identifies ONE correct step in the storage calculation
markerNotes: Award the working as well as the answer: pixels per frame, bytes per frame, frames per second, then the total.
Check that bytes are used throughout and that the total is converted using the 1,000,000 bytes per MB stated in the question.
The answer must be 829.4 MB to one decimal place, with units.
commonStudentErrors: Using 24 bits per pixel as 24 bytes, which overstates the storage eightfold.
Calculating the storage for one frame and not multiplying by the frames per second and the ten seconds.
Mixing units, such as using 1,024 x 1,024 bytes per megabyte when the question defines 1 MB as 1,000,000 bytes.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each frame has 1280 by 720 pixels, which is 921,600 pixels in total, and each pixel needs 3 bytes, so one frame needs 2,764,800 bytes. Because the video is uncompressed, every frame is stored in full. At 30 frames per second, one second needs 82,944,000 bytes, so ten seconds need 829,440,000 bytes. The storage needed is 829.4 megabytes (MB).
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the pixels, bytes per frame and total for ten seconds, and states 829.4 MB with working shown, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each frame has 921,600 pixels at 3 bytes each, so one frame needs 2,764,800 bytes. The full clip would need a much larger total.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the bytes for one frame correctly, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, calculate the total for ten seconds at 30 frames per second and state the storage in MB.

sampleAnswers.answer: The video is 1280 by 720 pixels, so each frame has 921,600 pixels.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one correct step, the pixels in each frame, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, calculate the bytes needed for one frame.

prompts.question: Justify whether one workstation with the same specification could run both the virtual reality (VR) training simulation and the museum kiosk, using their performance requirements.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a studio must select hardware for two interactive media projects. The first is a virtual reality (VR) training simulation for a mining company, which renders 3D scenes in real time at a frame rate of around 90 frames per second, a common target for comfortable VR. The second is a museum kiosk that plays pre-recorded video with touch-screen menus. The studio has the budget for only one workstation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies whether one workstation can meet both projects, weighing each project's hardware needs, and states the conditions
5 marks: Justifies the decision with relevant hardware reasons for both projects
4 marks: Compares the two projects' hardware needs, with some reasons for the choice
3 marks: Describes the hardware needs of one project, with some reference to the other
2 marks: Identifies a difference in hardware needs between the projects
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about hardware or frame rate
markerNotes: Justify by weighing each project's requirement against the other, then deciding whether one workstation meets both, with reasons.
Name specific components, such as the graphics card, memory and frame rate, rather than general claims about a powerful computer.
A conditional decision, such as 'only if the graphics card is chosen for the simulation', shows the judgement the top band needs.
commonStudentErrors: Saying both projects need 'a good computer' without naming the components that matter.
Describing the simulation's hardware without comparing it with the kiosk.
Concluding that one workstation is suitable without giving the graphics or memory evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: The virtual reality (VR) simulation has far higher hardware performance requirements than the kiosk. Real-time rendering of three-dimensional scenes needs a powerful graphics card and fast memory, and the frame rate must stay near 90 frames per second or users may experience discomfort. The kiosk plays pre-recorded video, which the processor can decode with modest graphics demand, and its touch menus need little processing. A single workstation could run both only if its graphics card is chosen for the simulation, because an underpowered card would make the VR experience stutter. Memory matters too, since the simulation holds 3D models and textures in RAM while the kiosk needs far less. Given the budget, a workstation specified for the simulation would be more than adequate for the kiosk, so one shared workstation is justified, provided the studio tests the simulation's frame rate before purchase.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Weighs the graphics, memory and frame rate needs of both projects and states the conditions for one workstation, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The VR simulation needs a powerful graphics card and a high frame rate, while the kiosk only plays video. A single workstation could run both if it has a strong enough graphics card, so the choice is reasonable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the two projects' hardware needs and gives a choice with a brief reason, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, justify the choice with hardware reasons for both projects.

sampleAnswers.answer: The simulation needs more hardware than the kiosk, so it is harder to run.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a difference in hardware needs, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe the hardware needs of one project with reference to the other.

dotPoints.description: Explain how interactive media systems can support creative processes (sandbox gaming; social media; digital creative commons)

prompts.question: Describe how sandbox gaming lets the student experiment during the creative process.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a Year 11 student is designing a town for a school project in a sandbox game. Later, the student plans to share the finished town on social media and to add music from a digital creative commons library.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes TWO distinct ways sandbox gaming supports experimentation, each linked to the student's town project
3 marks: Describes TWO ways a sandbox supports creativity, with one linked to the town project
2 marks: Describes ONE way the sandbox environment supports experimentation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about sandbox games or creativity
markerNotes: Describe the mechanism, such as undoing a change or testing a layout, rather than saying sandbox games are creative.
Link each mechanism to the student's town project and to the experimenting step of the creative process.
Two different mechanisms earn credit; the same idea in two wordings earns one.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what a sandbox game is without saying how it supports the creative process.
Stating that games are creative or fun without explaining the mechanism that makes them so.
Repeating one idea, such as trying designs, in two different wordings.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sandbox gaming supports the creative process because the student can experiment without penalty: a building can be placed, removed and rebuilt until the town layout works. Immediate visual feedback lets the student test how a design looks before committing to it, which encourages trial and error. Sharing the finished town on social media then invites comments that may prompt further revisions. Because each attempt is low-risk, sandbox gaming encourages iteration rather than a single attempt, and this repeated cycle of testing is central to creative work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two distinct mechanisms, trial without penalty and feedback from sharing, each linked to the student's town project, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: In a sandbox game, the student can build a town and change it whenever they want. This lets them try ideas.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one way, changing the town at will, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe a second way sandbox gaming supports creativity, linked to the town project.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sandbox games are fun and creative.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information that sandbox games are creative, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe one way the sandbox supports experimentation.

prompts.question: Compare how social media and the digital creative commons support this filmmaker's creative process, including the conditions she must meet, and weigh the risks of each to reach a conclusion.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a Year 11 filmmaker is making a short documentary about her school's garden. She plans to share early cuts on social media to gather feedback, and she wants background music from a digital creative commons library, where creators share music under Creative Commons licences.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Compares how social media and the digital creative commons support different stages of the filmmaker's process, including the licence conditions she must meet, weighing the risks and reaching a conclusion
5 marks: Compares both resources with relevant reasons, including licence conditions or feedback risks
4 marks: Compares the two resources with some relevant reasons
3 marks: Describes social media and the digital creative commons with some link to the filmmaker
2 marks: Identifies a benefit of each resource
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about social media or creative commons
markerNotes: Compare on the same basis, such as how each supports the review stage or the production stage, so that the differences are clear.
Use licence conditions, such as attribution or non-commercial use, as evidence on the creative commons side.
A conclusion about which resource matters at which stage shows the judgement the top band needs.
commonStudentErrors: Describing social media and the creative commons separately, without any direct comparison.
Assuming all creative commons material can be used in any way, without mentioning licence conditions.
Treating feedback from social media as always helpful, without noting that comments can be unhelpful.

sampleAnswers.answer: Social media and the digital creative commons both support the creative process, but at different stages. Social media supports the review stage: sharing early cuts gives the filmmaker rapid feedback from viewers, which lets her test whether scenes hold attention and revise before release. Its value depends on the quality of comments, and public posting can expose unfinished work to criticism. The digital creative commons supports the production stage by providing background music she can use without negotiating a separate licence for each track. However, a Creative Commons licence attaches conditions, such as attribution to the creator, and she must check whether a track allows commercial use if the documentary is later sold. Social media therefore helps her improve the work, while the digital creative commons helps her build it. Both are valuable only if she meets the licence conditions and weighs feedback critically.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the two resources by the stage each supports, weighing licence conditions and feedback risks, and reaches a conclusion, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Social media gives the filmmaker feedback on early cuts, which helps her revise the documentary. The digital creative commons provides music she can use, but she must follow the licence conditions, such as attribution.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares social media feedback with the licence conditions for music, with some reasons, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, develop the licence conditions and feedback risks with relevant reasons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Social media lets her share the film and get comments, and creative commons music is free to use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a benefit of each resource, which meets the 2-mark row, but the claim that creative commons music is free overlooks its licence conditions. To reach 3 marks, describe both resources with a link to the filmmaker.

dotPoints.description: Examine how human behaviour may be influenced by interactive media, including opportunities for people with disability to explore and participate in their environment

prompts.question: Describe how captions and a text transcript allow a visitor who is deaf or hard of hearing to explore the exhibits in the online video tour.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional museum adds an online video tour of its exhibits to its website. The tour uses spoken narration and on-screen text, and the museum wants visitors with disability to be able to explore and enjoy the exhibits as fully as other visitors.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes TWO accurate ways captions and a transcript let a visitor with hearing disability explore the exhibits, each linked to the tour
2 marks: Describes ONE accurate way captions or a transcript help a visitor with disability
1 mark: Identifies a feature of captions or a transcript
markerNotes: Describe how the feature removes a barrier, such as relying on sound, rather than simply naming captions.
Link the feature to exploring and participating in the museum tour, the wording used in the question.
Two distinct features, such as captions and a transcript, earn credit; two wordings of the same feature earn one.
commonStudentErrors: Naming captions without describing what they do for a visitor who is deaf or hard of hearing.
Saying captions help 'everyone' without identifying the barrier they remove for people with disability.
Confusing captions with audio description, which describes on-screen visuals for people who are blind or have low vision.

sampleAnswers.answer: Captions show the narration as on-screen text, so a visitor who is deaf or hard of hearing can follow the tour without relying on sound. A text transcript lets the visitor read at their own pace, and screen readers can read it aloud for people who are blind. Together these features allow people with disability to explore the exhibits and participate in the tour.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes captions and a transcript as two ways a visitor with hearing disability can follow and explore the tour, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Captions show the narration on screen, which helps a deaf visitor follow the tour.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one way captions help a deaf visitor, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe a transcript as a second way, linked to the online tour.

sampleAnswers.answer: Captions are useful for some visitors.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies captions as a feature, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe how the captions help a visitor with disability.

prompts.question: Examine how the app may influence residents' walking behaviour, and how its voice navigation allows residents with disability to explore and participate in the trails, and judge how far each of these effects can be relied on.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a city council launches a free mobile app that guides residents along its walking trails. The app sends push notifications at set times, counts steps, awards badges for weekly goals and offers voice navigation and high-contrast maps for residents with vision impairment.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Examines how the app may influence walking habits; Explains how voice navigation lets residents with disability explore and participate, with a balanced judgement
5 marks: Examines the influence on walking and the access benefits, with relevant reasons
4 marks: Examines one influence on walking and one accessibility feature, with some reasoning
3 marks: Describes the app's features and their likely effects on residents
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the app and a possible effect
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the app or walking
markerNotes: Examine by tracing a feature to its likely effect on behaviour, and say where the effect may be limited, such as novelty wearing off.
Treat accessibility as a design feature with an effect on participation, not as an add-on or a separate topic.
Qualify claims about behaviour, since influence is likely rather than certain; the strongest answers say so.
Answers could include: push notifications at set times; step counts; badges for weekly goals; voice navigation; high-contrast maps
commonStudentErrors: Stating that notifications 'make people exercise' without explaining how the feature works.
Describing voice navigation as useful for everyone, without linking it to residents with vision impairment.
Treating the behaviour and disability parts as separate topics, with no link between them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The app is interactive media that may influence human behaviour through its design. Push notifications prompt residents to walk at set times, and step counts show progress, which can build a regular walking habit. Badges give feedback that reinforces the habit, although the effect may fade once the novelty wears off, so the influence is not guaranteed. The app also affects access. Voice navigation gives turn-by-turn directions, so a resident with vision impairment can follow a trail without relying on a printed map, and high-contrast maps help others with low vision read the route. These features allow people with disability to explore and participate in the trails on equal terms with other residents. Overall, the app's influence on behaviour is positive for many residents, but its benefits depend on accessible design being treated as a core requirement rather than an optional extra.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Examines the walking influence of notifications and badges, and the access benefit of voice navigation, qualifying both and reaching a balanced judgement, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Push notifications and step counts may encourage residents to walk regularly, though the effect may fade. Voice navigation lets residents with vision impairment explore the trails without a printed map.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Examines one influence on walking and one accessibility feature, with some reasoning, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, examine both with relevant reasons in more depth.

sampleAnswers.answer: The app's rewards may make people walk more, and voice navigation helps some residents.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one feature, the rewards, and a possible effect on walking, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe the app's features and their likely effects on residents.

dotPoints.description: Investigate how digital marketing techniques influence consumer behaviour (guided choice (nudging); default settings, including cookies; autofill; pop-ups promoting online shopping)

prompts.question: Clarify how the pre-ticked 'send me offers' box can influence a customer's decision to receive marketing emails.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: an online clothing store's checkout page has the 'send me offers' box already ticked. Many customers complete the purchase without changing this box, and the store then sends them marketing emails for the following year.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Clarifies how the pre-ticked default influences customers through inertia and nudging, linked to the store's marketing and informed consent
3 marks: Clarifies the influence of the default setting on customers, with a clear link to the store
2 marks: Clarifies one effect of the pre-ticked box on customers, with a brief reason
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about digital marketing or default settings
markerNotes: Explain why the default works, such as customers not changing settings, rather than only naming the technique.
Link the default to the store's digital marketing aim, such as a larger mailing list.
An ethical point about informed consent shows the wider effect on the customer, which the top band expects.
commonStudentErrors: Naming 'default settings' or 'nudging' without clarifying how the pre-ticked box changes a decision.
Writing that the box 'forces' customers to accept, when the customer can untick it.
Confusing a default setting with a pop-up, which is a separate technique.

sampleAnswers.answer: Default settings are options that are already selected before the customer acts. The pre-ticked box influences consumer behaviour through inertia, because many customers do not change a setting, so they receive marketing emails they did not actively request. The store benefits from this digital marketing technique, since the default creates a larger mailing list without extra effort. The effect is a nudge towards accepting, which is why the default should be unticked if the customer's informed consent is to be genuine.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Clarifies the pre-ticked default through inertia and nudging, linked to the store's marketing and to informed consent, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The box is already ticked, so many customers will leave it as it is and receive emails.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Clarifies one effect, that customers leave the box ticked, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, link the default to the store's marketing and clarify its influence on the store.

sampleAnswers.answer: A pre-ticked box is a type of digital marketing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information that the box is a form of digital marketing, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, clarify one effect of the box on customers.

prompts.question: Analyse how the store's combined use of autofill, cookies and pop-ups may influence this customer's purchasing decision, and weigh the ethical risks of combining them.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a customer returns to an online shoe store on her phone. The store has saved her card details through autofill, and cookies show she browsed running shoes last week. A pop-up offering a limited-time discount appears just as she reaches the checkout.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how autofill, cookies and pop-ups each influence the purchase, weighing the ethical risks of combining them
5 marks: Analyses at least TWO mechanisms with clear links to the purchase
4 marks: Analyses TWO techniques with some links to consumer behaviour
3 marks: Describes the techniques and a likely effect on the customer
2 marks: Identifies a technique and a benefit to the customer or store
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about online shopping or pop-ups
markerNotes: Analyse the mechanism for each technique, such as removing effort or creating urgency, before judging how far it influences the purchase.
Link cookies to the pop-up, since the scenario uses browsing history to target the offer.
An ethical judgement, such as the need for disclosure or an easy opt-out, separates the top band from a description.
commonStudentErrors: Describing autofill, cookies and pop-ups as techniques without analysing how each changes the purchase.
Treating cookies as passwords or as a virus, rather than as small files that store browsing data.
Assuming every customer responds to pop-ups in the same way, without qualifying the influence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Autofill and pop-ups influence consumer behaviour through different mechanisms. Autofill removes the effort of entering card details, so the customer completes the purchase in fewer steps, and each removed step makes a purchase more likely. Pop-ups create urgency: a limited-time discount invites a decision before the customer has compared prices. Cookies support the approach by recording browsing history, so the store can match the pop-up to the running shoes she has already viewed. This digital marketing combination is effective because it reduces the time and deliberation the customer would otherwise spend. However, it also raises concerns. The customer may buy on impulse, and her browsing data is used in ways she may not expect, so the store should disclose its use of cookies and make it easy to decline. An ethical store would balance this commercial gain against the customer's ability to make an informed choice, and would avoid using stored data in ways that feel intrusive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the mechanism of autofill, cookies and pop-ups in turn, and weighs the ethical risks of combining them, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pop-ups create urgency with a limited-time discount, so the customer may decide quickly. Autofill makes checkout faster by filling in card details, which reduces effort.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses two techniques, pop-up urgency and autofill, with some links to behaviour, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, link the two techniques more clearly to the purchase decision.

sampleAnswers.answer: Autofill saves time, and pop-ups can offer discounts to customers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies autofill and a pop-up discount as techniques with a benefit, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe the likely effect on the customer's purchase.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate social media applications that encourage human connections (crowdsourcing through a social media app; learning via massive online open courses (MOOCs); gaming platforms that encourage massive multiplayer online games (MMOGs))

prompts.question: Classify each platform as crowdsourcing, a massive online open course (MOOC) or a massive multiplayer online game (MMOG), and give one feature that supports each classification.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a school project compares three online platforms. Platform X is a social media app where residents submit and rate footpath problems, which the council uses to prioritise repairs. Platform Y offers a free course on local history that thousands of learners can enrol in. Platform Z is a fantasy world where thousands of players interact in one persistent online space.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies all three platforms correctly, each with a feature that supports the classification
2 marks: Classifies TWO of the three platforms correctly, each with a supporting feature
1 mark: Classifies ONE platform correctly OR names a correct feature of one platform
markerNotes: Check each category against its defining feature: contributions from many people, open enrolment for large numbers, or persistent play for many players at once.
A classification with a supporting feature, such as open enrolment or one shared world, earns more than a bare label.
Keep each supporting feature to one clause; the question asks for classification, not a full analysis.
commonStudentErrors: Classifying a platform by its popularity or age rather than by its defining feature.
Confusing MOOCs, which are courses, with MMOGs, which are games played in a persistent online world.
Giving a category without any feature that supports it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Platform X is crowdsourcing: residents contribute footpath reports through a social media app, and the council uses their input to rank repairs. Platform Y offers massive online open courses, since its free course is open to thousands of enrolled learners. Platform Z hosts massive multiplayer online games, where players form human connections in one shared world.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all three platforms correctly, each with a supporting feature, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Platform X is an example of crowdsourcing, since residents supply the reports. Platform Y offers a massive online open course, because the course is free and open.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies two platforms correctly, each with a supporting feature, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, classify Platform Z as a massive multiplayer online game with a supporting feature.

sampleAnswers.answer: Platform X is an example of crowdsourcing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies one platform correctly, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, classify a second platform with a supporting feature.

prompts.question: Evaluate how effectively the three options build human connections among the students.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a high school is deciding how to help students connect with their community and with each other. The three options are a crowdsourcing app built into the school's social media page for a community-history project, a free online course with thousands of enrolled learners, and a team-based game in which students cooperate in a persistent online world. Teachers are concerned about cyber safety, the accuracy of content and whether online connections are meaningful.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates all three options against the goal of human connections, weighing benefits and risks, and reaches a supported judgement
5 marks: Evaluates at least TWO options with relevant benefits and risks, weighed against connection
4 marks: Evaluates TWO options, with some reasons for their benefits and risks
3 marks: Describes at least TWO of the options and their connection benefits
2 marks: Identifies ONE option with a benefit OR a risk
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about online platforms and connection
markerNotes: Evaluate by weighing each option's benefit for connection against its risks, then judging which is most effective and why.
Refer to the school's goal of building connection, so the judgement answers the question rather than discussing social media in general.
Name the feature that creates each connection, such as team play, forum discussion or contributions to a shared map.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each option without judging how effective it is at building human connections.
Assuming online connections are always weaker or stronger than face-to-face ones, without evidence.
Ignoring risks, such as cyber safety or inaccurate content, when evaluating.

sampleAnswers.answer: A crowdsourcing app creates human connections between students and community members, who supply and check local information together. Its effectiveness depends on moderation, because open contributions on social media may include inaccurate content and unkind comments. Massive online open courses offer content that is often developed by universities and let students learn at their own pace, but they often provide weak human connections, since interaction is mostly through forums with thousands of other learners. Massive multiplayer online games encourage strong connections, because teams cooperate in real time and friendships can continue offline. However, these games carry cyber safety risks and may distract from learning if they are not structured. On balance, the crowdsourcing option is most effective for community connection if it is moderated, the game is best for teamwork if supervised, and the course is strongest for content but weakest for connection.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates each option's connection benefits against its risks, and judges which is most effective, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A crowdsourcing app connects students with community members, which builds communication skills. However, the content may be inaccurate without moderation. Massive multiplayer online games encourage teamwork, though they raise cyber safety concerns.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates two options, each with a benefit and a risk, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, weigh those benefits and risks against connection.

sampleAnswers.answer: The game is fun and helps students make friends, but it might be unsafe.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one option with a benefit and a risk, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe all three options and their connection benefits.

dotPoints.description: Explore how interactive media platforms support the creation of digital identities (personal e-profiles; identifier versus identity; profiling and auto-profiling; privacy settings)

prompts.question: Outline the difference between an identifier and an identity, and give one example of each from a social media account.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has a social media account with a username, a profile that lists her school and hobbies, and a history of posts and followers. Her friends mostly use her username to find her, while her profile describes who she is online.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the difference between an identifier and an identity; Gives an accurate example of each from the social media account
2 marks: Defines an identifier and an identity, OR gives an example of each term
1 mark: Describes one of the terms briefly
markerNotes: Define an identifier as a label that distinguishes one account from another, and an identity as the wider set of information linked to a person.
The example should show each term in use, such as a username and the profile attached to it, rather than a general statement.
One clear sentence per term plus an example is enough for three marks; extra detail does not add marks.
commonStudentErrors: Treating identifier and identity as the same thing, such as calling a username a digital identity.
Defining identity without naming an identifier or stating how the two differ.
Describing privacy settings instead of the identifier and identity the question asks about.

sampleAnswers.answer: An identifier is a label that tells a platform which account is which, such as a username or email address. An identity is the wider set of information linked to a person, such as profile details, interests and activity. For example, on a social media account the username is an identifier, while the profile and posts linked to it form part of the student's digital identity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines both terms, states the difference, and gives a clear example of each from the account, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: An identifier is a username or email address used to find an account. An identity is the information about a person that a platform holds, such as their profile and interests.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines both terms, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, state the difference between them and give an example of each from the social media account.

sampleAnswers.answer: An identity is the profile a student builds on a social media site.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one term, identity, briefly, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, define both terms.

prompts.question: Analyse how profiling and auto-profiling on an interactive media platform shape a user's digital identity, including the limits of privacy settings.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 student uses a photo-sharing platform. She has listed her school and hobbies on her profile, has liked many travel posts and searches for hiking gear, and has set her friends list to private.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how profiling and auto-profiling shape the digital identity; Explains the limits of privacy settings
4 marks: Analyses how profiling or auto-profiling shapes the digital identity; Notes a limit of privacy settings
3 marks: Describes profiling or auto-profiling, with some link to the digital identity
2 marks: Identifies profiling OR privacy settings, with a brief comment on the digital identity
1 mark: Names a relevant term from digital identity
markerNotes: Separate profiling (information the user supplies) from auto-profiling (attributes inferred from behaviour) before linking both to the digital identity.
Use the scenario's details, such as the liked posts and hiking searches, as evidence rather than retelling the scenario.
The strongest answers show that privacy settings control visibility, not the platform's data collection or inferences.
commonStudentErrors: Describing privacy settings as complete protection that stops all data collection.
Using profiling and auto-profiling as if they were the same process.
Listing platform features without explaining how they build the student's digital identity.

sampleAnswers.answer: On an interactive media platform, profiling builds a picture of a user from information the user supplies, such as the school and hobbies on a profile. Auto-profiling goes further by inferring attributes the student never entered, such as an interest in outdoor activities, from behaviour like the travel posts she likes and the hiking gear she searches for. Together these processes build a digital identity that she may not fully recognise, and the platform uses it to choose the content and advertising she sees. Privacy settings, such as a private friends list, control who can see shared information, but they may not stop the platform collecting behaviour or drawing inferences from it. The limits of privacy settings therefore leave part of her digital identity beyond her direct control.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses profiling and auto-profiling separately and their effect on the identity, and explains the limits of privacy settings, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Auto-profiling uses the likes and searches on a platform to guess a user's interests, which shapes the digital identity the platform builds. Privacy settings can hide the friends list from other users.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes auto-profiling with some link to the digital identity, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, analyse how auto-profiling shapes the identity and note a limit of privacy settings.

sampleAnswers.answer: Auto-profiling and privacy settings are features of platforms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names two relevant terms without explaining how they shape the digital identity, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify profiling or privacy settings with a comment on the identity.

dotPoints.description: Select and use appropriate file formats for a defined purpose

prompts.question: Apply your knowledge of file formats to select a suitable format for each of the three assets in the scenario, giving one reason for each choice.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 team is building an interactive museum guide for a web browser. The three assets are a 2 MB colour photograph of a historic ship that will be shown full-screen, a company logo that must sit over coloured backgrounds without a white box, and a 30-second music loop that must play smoothly on a phone.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Selects a suitable format for all three assets, with a reason for each that links the format to its purpose
3 marks: Selects a suitable format for all three assets, with reasons for TWO of them
2 marks: Selects a suitable format for all three assets, OR selects TWO correctly with a reason for each
1 mark: Names a suitable file format for one asset
markerNotes: Match each format to the purpose of its asset: the photograph needs quality and a small size, the logo needs transparency, and the music needs compression.
Give a reason for each format, such as lossy compression for file size or transparency support, to move beyond a simple list.
An SVG logo is also a valid choice because vector files scale without losing quality; accept it if the reason is given.
Answers could include: JPEG for the photograph; PNG or SVG for the logo; MP3 or AAC for the music loop
commonStudentErrors: Choosing a lossless format such as PNG for the photograph without considering file size.
Naming a format for each asset without giving any reason.
Describing JPEG as a lossless format.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each choice depends on the defined purpose of the asset. The photograph should be saved as a JPEG, because JPEG uses lossy compression to shrink a 2 MB colour image into a file that displays quickly full-screen. The logo should be a PNG, because PNG is lossless and supports transparency, so it sits cleanly over coloured backgrounds without a white box. An SVG would also suit the logo, since vector file formats scale without losing quality. The music loop should be an MP3, because this compressed audio format produces a much smaller file than an uncompressed WAV, which helps it play smoothly on a phone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Selects a suitable format for each asset with a reason linked to its purpose, such as lossy compression for the photograph, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Use a JPEG for the photograph, a PNG for the logo and an MP3 for the music loop.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Selects a suitable format for all three assets, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, give a reason for two of the formats, linked to their purpose.

sampleAnswers.answer: The photograph should be a JPEG file.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names a suitable format for one asset, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, select a suitable format for all three assets.

prompts.question: Analyse why the museum would keep a lossless master copy of the photograph in one file format while publishing a compressed copy in another format for the same exhibition.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional museum digitises a fragile 1920s photograph for an online exhibition. The museum needs a high-quality archive copy for future printing and editing, while the exhibition website must load quickly on mobile devices.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the trade-off between a lossless master and a lossy copy, showing each serves a different purpose for the photograph
4 marks: Analyses the difference between lossless and lossy formats, linking one of them clearly to its purpose
3 marks: Explains that the two formats store data differently, with a general link to archiving or web delivery
2 marks: Describes one format and its file size or quality, with a brief reference to its purpose
1 mark: Names a file format or compression type
markerNotes: Explain the trade-off in terms of purpose: the master protects the original for editing and printing, while the compressed copy makes the website fast on phones.
Lossless means the original data can be rebuilt exactly; lossy means data is permanently discarded, so each re-save of a lossy file loses more quality.
Link each file format to a specific use rather than only defining the two compression types.
Answers could include: PNG or TIFF as lossless master formats; JPEG as the lossy web copy
commonStudentErrors: Saying that a JPEG keeps the image exactly, or that lossless files are always the smaller choice.
Describing lossy and lossless compression without saying why the museum would use each copy.
Suggesting the compressed copy should replace the master, so the archive is no longer needed.

sampleAnswers.answer: The museum keeps a lossless master copy, such as a PNG or TIFF file, because lossless compression can rebuild the original image exactly, so every detail of the 1920s photograph is preserved. The archive can then be edited, reprinted at high resolution or converted to other file formats later without any loss of quality. The website copy is a lossy JPEG, which discards some image information to reduce file size, so the exhibition page loads quickly on mobile devices. Each time a JPEG is re-saved, a little more quality is lost, which is why the master is never published or re-saved as a JPEG. The two copies serve different purposes: the master protects the original for preservation, and the compressed copy delivers the photograph efficiently to the public.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the lossless master against the lossy web copy in terms of their purposes, and explains the loss from re-saving, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The master is a lossless PNG, so the photograph keeps all its detail for future editing. The website copy is a lossy JPEG, which is smaller, so it downloads faster. Both files are needed for different uses.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the two formats with a general link to editing and downloading, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, analyse the difference between lossless and lossy formats and link one of them clearly to its purpose.

sampleAnswers.answer: The museum uses a PNG for the master and a JPEG for the website.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names two formats, a PNG and a JPEG, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe one format and its file size or quality, with a reference to its purpose.

dotPoints.description: Use software to develop elements of interactive media in a project

prompts.question: Describe how a developer could use authoring software to build two interactive elements for the project: a navigation menu and a pop-up information panel.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 team is building a web-based interactive map of a local heritage walk for a council project. The map needs a navigation menu that opens each stop, and an information panel that appears when a visitor clicks a location marker.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how the navigation menu and pop-up panel are each built and triggered in the software, and how each responds to the user
2 marks: Describes both elements in general terms, with a brief mention of how the software makes them work
1 mark: Identifies one element or software feature used in the project
markerNotes: Name the software feature that makes each element work, such as an event, action or trigger, rather than only naming the element.
Describe the steps the developer takes, such as building the element and then setting when it responds.
Connect the answer to the heritage walk scenario so the elements are shown as parts of the project.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a menu or a panel without saying how the authoring software makes it work.
Describing the colours and layout of the interface rather than the interactive behaviour built in the software.
Writing program code when the question asks how the authoring software is used.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the authoring software, the developer builds the navigation menu as a set of buttons, each with an on-click event that jumps to the matching stop. The pop-up information panel is created as a hidden layer that is set to appear only when its location marker is clicked. The developer then sets a trigger that changes the panel's visibility, and tests both elements in preview mode before the interactive media project is published.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes how the menu and panel are each built and triggered in the software, with an event or trigger for each, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The developer can make buttons for each stop in the software and link each button to its page. A pop-up panel can be hidden until a marker is clicked.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both elements in general terms, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, name the software feature that makes each element work, such as an event or trigger.

sampleAnswers.answer: A navigation menu can be made using buttons in the software.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one element, the navigation menu, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe both elements in general terms and how the software makes them work.

prompts.question: Explain how testing each interactive element separately, before combining the elements, helps the team identify and fix faults in the interactive media project.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The heritage walk team has built a navigation menu, a pop-up information panel and a photo slideshow as separate elements. It is now combining them into one web page for the council, and the menu links do not yet open the correct pages.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains how testing each element separately isolates a fault's source, and how early fixing stops faults spreading in the combined project
4 marks: Explains how separate testing isolates faults in individual elements, with a clear link to the combined project
3 marks: Explains one benefit of testing elements separately, with a general link to the project
2 marks: Describes testing in general terms, with a brief mention of faults in the project
1 mark: Identifies testing or faults in the project
markerNotes: The key idea is isolation: testing one element alone narrows the search for a fault when the elements are combined.
Refer to the navigation menu and the combined web page so the explanation uses the scenario.
Link early fault-finding to the cost of fixing errors in a larger, combined project.
commonStudentErrors: Saying testing finds all faults, without explaining why testing elements separately helps.
Listing the steps of testing without explaining how testing one element alone helps locate a fault.
Describing testing as a general quality check without linking it to the combined project.

sampleAnswers.answer: Testing each element separately isolates the source of a fault, so the team can tell where a problem begins. If the navigation menu fails when it is tested alone, the fault must lie in the menu's own settings or in the pages it links to. If the links only fail after the elements are combined, the cause is more likely to be a conflict between elements, such as a hidden panel covering the menu. Without separate testing, both possibilities would appear as one fault somewhere on the page, and the team would have to search the whole web page. Fixing each element while it is still small and self-contained stops errors spreading into the others, so the finished interactive media project works as intended and is quicker to debug.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how separate testing isolates the source of a fault, using the navigation menu, and links early fixing to the combined project, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Testing the navigation menu alone shows whether its links work, so a fault can be traced to that element. This helps the team fix the problem before the element is combined with the other elements of the project.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains one benefit, that a fault can be traced to the menu, with a general link to the project, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, explain how separate testing isolates faults in each element, with a clear link to the combined project.

sampleAnswers.answer: Testing is important because it finds faults in the project.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies testing and faults in the project, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe testing in general terms and how it finds faults.

dotPoints.description: Use hardware and software to digitise assets for use in interactive media systems, including lossy and lossless data compression

prompts.question: Calculate the uncompressed file size of the clip in megabytes, the size of the same clip saved as a 128 kbps MP3, and the approximate compression ratio.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student records a 30-second stereo sound effect for an interactive quiz at a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz with a bit depth of 16 bits. She then saves a copy as an MP3 at a constant bit rate of 128 kbps. Use 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes, 1 byte = 8 bits and 1 kbps = 1,000 bits per second.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Calculates both file sizes correctly in megabytes, with working shown at each step, and a correct compression ratio
3 marks: Calculates both file sizes correctly, with working shown
2 marks: Calculates the uncompressed file size correctly, with working shown
1 mark: States the file size formula, or substitutes some values into it
markerNotes: Show every step with units: samples per second, multiplied by bit depth and channels, multiplied by time, then divided by 8 to get bytes.
Use the values given in the scenario and the stated unit conversions; a correct method with a unit error loses marks.
The compression ratio is the uncompressed size divided by the compressed size, and the answer should note that MP3 is lossy.
Answers could include: about 5.3 MB uncompressed; about 0.48 MB as an MP3; a compression ratio of about 11 to 1
commonStudentErrors: Forgetting to multiply by the number of channels, which gives half the correct uncompressed size.
Dividing bits by 8 incorrectly or mixing up megabytes and megabits.
Stating a formula but never substituting the values from the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Uncompressed size: sampling rate 44,100 samples per second multiplied by bit depth 16 bits multiplied by 2 channels gives 1,411,200 bits per second.
