prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a Year 11 start-up team has a plan to sell its app to schools for a fixed annual fee. Its members differ in confidence, with some keen to adapt quickly after setbacks and others preferring to plan every step before acting.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a reasoned position on which factor contributes more, with sustained links to success and a qualified conclusion
5 marks: Justifies a clear position with links to success for both factors
4 marks: Explains how a clear business model and the cultural characteristics each contribute to success, with a stated position
3 marks: Explains one business or cultural characteristic and its contribution to the start-up, with some reference to the other
2 marks: Identifies a business or cultural characteristic relevant to start-ups
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about start-ups
markerNotes: Justify a position on which factor contributes more, then show why the other factor still matters, rather than describing both equally.
Use the scenario's details, such as the fixed annual fee and the team's differing confidence, to test each factor.
A qualified conclusion, such as the factors working together, is stronger than one that dismisses the other factor.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the business model and the cultural characteristics without taking a position on which contributes more.
Declaring one factor more important with no reasons or link to success.
Treating resilience and openness as business characteristics rather than individual cultural characteristics.

sampleAnswers.answer: For a start-up, a clear business model contributes more to success, although the individual cultural characteristics of resilience and openness are needed to deliver it. A fixed annual fee gives the team predictable income and a direct test of whether schools will pay. Without a model like this, even a resilient team may spend its time on features nobody buys. The model also sets targets that guide decisions about what to build and when to launch. The cultural characteristics, however, determine whether the model can be delivered. Resilience lets the team recover from failed trials, and openness lets members accept criticism from schools and change the product. A team that is not resilient may abandon the venture at its first setback, while one that is closed to feedback will ignore evidence on whether schools will pay. These characteristics cannot replace a viable market. On balance, the business model is the stronger factor in the first year, so the team should treat resilience and openness as conditions for that model.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Takes a position that the business model contributes more, justifies it with links to success, and treats resilience and openness as conditions, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A business model is important because a fixed annual fee shows whether schools will pay for the app. Resilience and openness help the team cope with setbacks and listen to feedback. On balance the business model matters most, although both are needed for the start-up's success.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how the business model and the cultural characteristics each contribute to success, with a stated position, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, justify the position with links to success for both factors.

sampleAnswers.answer: A business model is needed to earn money. Resilience is a cultural characteristic that helps people keep going.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a business model and resilience as relevant characteristics, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain how one of them contributes to the start-up's success.

subTopics.name: Storage and workflow in enterprise networks

dotPoints.description: Investigate how the developments in network connectivity and speed have influenced work practices within an enterprise (remote working opportunities; file sharing; task delegation and monitoring)

prompts.question: Summarise how this improvement in network connectivity and speed has changed the work practices of the enterprise, particularly remote working and file sharing.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a design agency of 25 staff has upgraded from a slow broadband connection to a faster fibre connection. It now uses cloud-based file sharing, and some staff work from home two days a week.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Summarises the main changes to work practices from faster connectivity, covering remote working and file sharing, with a clear overall statement
3 marks: Summarises changes to remote working and file sharing, with links to the agency
2 marks: Identifies one change in work practices caused by faster connectivity
1 mark: Makes a general statement about faster internet
markerNotes: A summary states the main points briefly; the marker is looking for the change in practice, not the technical detail of the network.
Name the practices affected, such as remote working and file sharing, and tie each one to the upgrade in connectivity or speed.
A closing statement that draws the points together shows the answer has been summarised rather than listed.
commonStudentErrors: Describing fibre cables and broadband technology in detail, rather than the change in work practices.
Writing general benefits of the internet without referring to the agency's upgrade.
Listing remote working and file sharing as separate points without saying how the faster speed affects them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The improved network connectivity and speed have made remote working practical for the enterprise, because staff at home can open large design files and join video meetings without long delays. Cloud-based file sharing supports this by giving every staff member the same current version of each project, whether in the office or at home. Before the upgrade, large files had to be emailed or copied to a shared drive, which was slow and risked version conflicts. In summary, the agency has moved from office-bound work practices to shared, anywhere-access ones, which depend on a reliable connection.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Remote working and file sharing are both summarised with links to the upgrade, and an overall statement closes the answer, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Staff can now work from home because the internet is faster, so remote working has improved for the agency.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one change, remote working, linked to the faster internet, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, add file sharing and link both changes to the agency.

sampleAnswers.answer: Faster internet is good for businesses because it makes everything quicker.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement that faster internet is good for businesses, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify one change in the agency's work practices.

prompts.question: Compare the task delegation and monitoring of office staff with those of remote staff, now that faster network connectivity supports remote working, and reach a reasoned conclusion on the trade-offs.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the agency assigns design tasks through a shared project board. Office staff are supervised in person, while remote staff's progress is tracked through the board, timestamped file uploads and a monitoring tool that logs activity on company laptops.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Compares delegation and monitoring for office and remote staff, with sustained links to connectivity, and reaches a reasoned conclusion on the trade-offs
5 marks: Compares both groups on delegation and monitoring with clear links to connectivity
4 marks: Explains the differences in monitoring between office and remote staff, with relevant links to the network
3 marks: Describes monitoring or task delegation for one group, with some reference to the other
2 marks: Identifies a monitoring method or delegation tool used by the agency
1 mark: Makes a general statement about remote working
markerNotes: Compare both groups on the same criteria, such as how tasks are assigned and how progress is checked, rather than describing each group separately.
Name the monitoring methods in the scenario and say what each one shows managers about the work.
A conclusion that weighs the trade-offs, such as monitoring activity against measuring outcomes, is what separates the top rows.
commonStudentErrors: Describing office and remote staff separately without making a comparison on the same criteria.
Calling the activity log a monitoring method without saying what it shows the managers.
Assuming monitoring is always a problem, rather than weighing its benefits against its effect on staff.

sampleAnswers.answer: Office and remote staff both receive tasks through the shared project board, so task delegation is consistent across the enterprise. The difference lies in monitoring. Office staff are supervised in person, so a manager can see progress and give immediate feedback. Remote staff are monitored through the board, timestamped uploads and an activity log, which gives managers a detailed record but says little about the quality of the work. Improved network connectivity makes both approaches workable. Faster connections let remote staff upload large files quickly, so their output is visible to managers almost as soon as it is ready, which narrows the gap between the two groups. The activity log, however, is a more intrusive form of monitoring and may lower trust. A fairer comparison uses outcomes such as deadlines met and quality of work, which support remote working better than activity counts alone, and this choice shapes the agency's work practices.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares delegation and monitoring for office and remote staff on shared criteria, with links to connectivity, and weighs the trade-off in its conclusion, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Office staff are monitored in person, so managers can give feedback straight away. Remote staff are monitored through the project board and an activity log, which can show when work happened. Both groups receive tasks through the board, but remote monitoring relies on the connection and is more formal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the differences in monitoring between office and remote staff, with links to the network, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, compare both groups on delegation and monitoring with clear links to connectivity.

sampleAnswers.answer: Office staff are watched by their manager. Remote staff use a project board and an activity log.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two monitoring methods, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe how one group's monitoring works, with some reference to the other.

dotPoints.description: Examine the benefits and limitations of digital workflows operating in an enterprise

prompts.question: Construct a digital workflow for this invoice approval process, set out as numbered steps that show who is responsible for each step.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a small builders' firm approves supplier invoices on paper. The office manager receives each invoice and passes it to the site supervisor to sign, and then the owner signs it before payment. Invoices are often lost between desks, and payments are late.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Constructs a complete digital workflow with numbered steps from receipt to payment, showing who is responsible for each step and how approvals are routed
3 marks: Constructs a workflow with most steps in logical order and clear routing
2 marks: Identifies some steps of the invoice approval process, OR constructs some steps in order
1 mark: Makes a general statement that digital systems speed up payments
markerNotes: Each step should show what happens and who acts, so the marker can follow the flow from invoice receipt to payment.
Name the digital feature doing the work, such as automatic routing or an electronic approval, rather than describing the paper process.
Keep the steps in logical order; the owner's approval cannot come before the supervisor has approved the invoice.
commonStudentErrors: Keeping a paper step, such as printing the invoice, in a workflow that is meant to be digital.
Listing steps without saying who is responsible for each one.
Placing payment before the owner's approval, which breaks the approval sequence.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The digital workflow for invoice approval in this enterprise is set out below as numbered steps:
1. The supplier invoice is emailed to a shared inbox, and the office manager logs it in the accounts system.
2. The system routes the invoice to the site supervisor, who approves it electronically once the work is confirmed as complete.
3. The system then routes the approved invoice to the owner, who gives final approval.
4. Each approval is time-stamped in an audit trail, so no invoice can be paid without both approvals.
5. The office manager releases the fully approved invoice for payment on its due date.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Sets out a complete numbered workflow from receipt to payment, showing who acts at each step and how approvals are routed, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: 1. The invoice is entered into the system. 2. The owner checks it and releases payment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two steps in order, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, add the supervisor's approval before the owner's, and name who acts at each step.

sampleAnswers.answer: Digital systems make payments faster, so the firm should use one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement that digital systems speed up payments, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify some steps of the invoice approval process.

prompts.question: Analyse how the features of this digital workflow create both benefits and limitations for the enterprise, including the supervisor's approvals on a weak mobile signal.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the builders' firm adopts the digital workflow. The workflow sends each invoice to the site supervisor for approval, then to the owner, time-stamps each approval, and holds payment until both are recorded. The owner is pleased that invoices are tracked, but the site supervisor is often away from the site and must approve invoices on a phone with a weak mobile signal.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how specific features, including the supervisor's approvals on a weak mobile signal, produce both benefits and limitations for the firm, with sustained cause and effect and a clear combined effect
5 marks: Analyses the workflow's benefits and limitations with clear links to its features and the firm
4 marks: Explains at least one benefit and one limitation of the workflow, with relevant links to the firm
3 marks: Explains one benefit or one limitation of the workflow, with some reference to the firm's situation
2 marks: Identifies a benefit or limitation of digital workflows
1 mark: Makes a general statement about digital systems
markerNotes: Link each benefit or limitation to the feature that causes it, such as the audit trail or the routing to one approver.
Use the scenario's details, such as the supervisor's weak phone signal, to test the workflow rather than general claims about digital systems.
Explain how a limitation changes a benefit, such as how a delayed approval reduces the timeliness the workflow was meant to provide.
commonStudentErrors: Listing benefits and limitations without linking either to a feature of the workflow.
Describing the paper process rather than the digital workflow.
Calling the audit trail a limitation, when it is a benefit that supports checking.

sampleAnswers.answer: The digital workflow creates benefits for the enterprise because each feature addresses a cause of the paper process's failures. Routing invoices automatically to the supervisor and the owner removes lost paperwork between desks, and the time-stamped audit trail shows who approved each invoice and when. Because payment cannot be released until both approvals are recorded, the system also reduces the risk of paying invoices without authority. These features make payments more timely and easier to check. The same features create limitations. Approval depends on the supervisor being able to act from a phone, so a weak mobile signal can stall an invoice and delay the payments the system was meant to speed up. The owner also receives every approval request, which makes one person a bottleneck who may be unavailable. The firm gains timeliness and accountability at the cost of dependence on connectivity and on each approver being available.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Links specific features to both benefits and limitations, and shows how the weak signal undermines timeliness, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The workflow tracks invoices, so the firm knows where each one is, and the audit trail shows who approved each invoice. This is a benefit. However, the supervisor's weak phone signal is a limitation, because approvals may be late.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains a benefit and a limitation with links to the firm, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, analyse the features that cause each one and link them to the firm's approvals.

sampleAnswers.answer: A digital workflow is quicker than paper. It can have problems if the internet does not work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a benefit and a limitation of digital workflows, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain one benefit or limitation with reference to the firm's situation.

dotPoints.description: Investigate data storage requirements for an enterprise (capacity; accessibility; location; security)

prompts.question: Calculate the total storage capacity the group needs for seven years of records, including 20% spare capacity, and state the figure the enterprise should plan for.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a group of 12 dental clinics generates 2 GB of patient records and scanned images per clinic each year. The group's policy is to keep each year's records for seven years, and it wants 20% spare capacity for growth.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Calculates the total capacity correctly as 201.6 GB, with each step shown and the capacity to plan for stated
3 marks: Calculates the seven-year total and the spare capacity correctly, with the final figure stated
2 marks: Calculates the yearly data or the seven-year total correctly
1 mark: Makes a basic calculation of one clinic's data
markerNotes: Show each step, such as the yearly total, the seven-year total and the 20% allowance, so the marker can see where any error occurs.
Apply the 20% to the seven-year total, not to the yearly figure, because the group must hold seven years of records.
Give the final answer with its unit, since a figure without GB is not a usable capacity requirement.
Answers could include: 24 GB of new data each year; 168 GB over seven years; 33.6 GB spare capacity; 201.6 GB in total
commonStudentErrors: Applying the 20% spare capacity to the yearly 24 GB instead of the seven-year total.
Multiplying one clinic's 2 GB by seven years and ignoring the other eleven clinics.
Rounding 201.6 GB down to 201 GB, which leaves the group short of capacity.

sampleAnswers.answer: Yearly storage: 12 clinics × 2 GB = 24 GB of new data each year. Seven years of records: 24 GB × 7 = 168 GB, because each year's data adds to the previous years. Spare capacity: 20% of 168 GB = 33.6 GB, which covers growth such as new clinics or larger scanned images. Total capacity required: 168 GB + 33.6 GB = 201.6 GB. The group should therefore plan for at least 201.6 GB of data storage, so that the storage requirements of the enterprise are met for the full seven years.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each step is shown from yearly data to the seven-year total, the 20% allowance is applied to the total, and the planning figure is stated with its unit, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each year the 12 clinics create 24 GB, so over seven years the group needs 168 GB of storage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the yearly data and the seven-year total correctly, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, add 20% spare capacity to the seven-year total and state the final figure.

sampleAnswers.answer: One clinic creates 2 GB of records each year, which is a modest amount to store.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a basic calculation of one clinic's yearly data, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, multiply by the 12 clinics or by seven years.

prompts.question: Recommend a storage arrangement for the group's records, weighing capacity, accessibility, location and security.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a group of 12 clinics currently keeps records on local computers at each site, which makes records hard to share between clinics. The group's IT manager must choose between a cloud storage service hosted in an Australian data centre and a network-attached storage (NAS) unit kept in the group's central office.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Recommends a storage arrangement, weighing capacity, accessibility, location and security, with a justified judgement on the conditions it depends on
5 marks: Recommends a storage arrangement with clear links to the four factors
4 marks: Explains how the options differ on two or three of the factors, with a recommendation stated
3 marks: Explains one factor for the options, with some reference to the group's needs
2 marks: Identifies a storage factor relevant to the group
1 mark: Makes a general statement about cloud storage
markerNotes: Weigh the four factors against each other for the clinic group, rather than describing each option in turn.
Name the conditions a recommendation depends on, such as encryption and access controls, so the judgement is tested.
Note where the other option would be the better choice, which shows the recommendation is reasoned.
commonStudentErrors: Describing cloud storage and NAS units in general terms without weighing them for the clinics.
Recommending an option without saying how it meets accessibility or security for the records.
Treating location as a minor factor, when the records' hosting location affects compliance checks.

sampleAnswers.answer: For this enterprise, I recommend cloud-based data storage hosted in an Australian data centre as the primary store, with a regular copy kept at the central office. Capacity favours the cloud, because the group needs about 202 GB for seven years of records and a cloud service can grow as clinics are added without buying new hardware. Accessibility also favours the cloud: every clinic can reach the same records over a secure internet connection, whereas a NAS unit would need a secure connection set up for each site. Location and security need conditions. An Australian data centre keeps records in a known location, which may simplify compliance checks on patient information. Security depends on encryption, access controls and multi-factor login, so the group must confirm the provider's controls before signing. A NAS unit gives physical control, but it concentrates risk in one office, where a fire or theft could remove the only copy unless backups are kept elsewhere. The cloud service with a local copy therefore offers the best balance, provided access is managed carefully.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Weighs capacity, accessibility, location and security for the clinics, and ties the recommendation to explicit conditions and the named risk of the alternative, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A cloud service gives the clinics more capacity and lets every site access the same records. A NAS unit in the central office keeps the records under the group's control, but it is harder for clinics to reach. Both options need good security. I would choose the cloud service because the records are easier to access.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how the options differ on capacity and accessibility, with a stated recommendation, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, link the recommendation clearly to all four factors, including location and security.

sampleAnswers.answer: A cloud service can hold more records than a NAS unit. Security matters for the group's records.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two storage factors, capacity and security, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain one factor for the two options with reference to the group's needs.

dotPoints.description: Explore cloud computing services (Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS); Software as a Service (SaaS); Platform as a Service (PaaS))

prompts.question: Apply the categories Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS) and Software as a Service (SaaS) to options (a), (b) and (c), explaining which party manages the operating system in each case.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a school's IT team is choosing among three cloud computing services. Option (a) rents virtual servers, on which the school installs and manages its own operating system and database. Option (b) provides a development environment where the school writes and deploys its own web app without managing any servers. Option (c) provides an online timetabling and email application that staff use in a browser.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Applies IaaS, PaaS and SaaS correctly to all three options, explaining for each which party manages the operating system and why
3 marks: Applies two categories correctly with the operating system explained, OR applies all three with most explanations complete
2 marks: Identifies the categories of one or two options, with some explanation of who manages the operating system
1 mark: Makes a general statement about cloud computing services
markerNotes: Match each option to its category by how much the provider manages, not by the name of the service.
For the operating system question, the school manages it only when the category is IaaS.
Name each category in full with its abbreviation at least once, so the marker can see the classification clearly.
commonStudentErrors: Classifying the browser-based timetabling service as PaaS because it is accessed over the internet.
Saying the school manages the operating system in PaaS, which the provider manages.
Matching an option to a category by its cost or size, rather than by which party manages what.

sampleAnswers.answer: The three options are cloud computing services that differ in how much the school manages. Option (a) is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): the provider supplies virtual servers, storage and networking, while the school installs and manages its own operating system and database. Option (b) is Platform as a Service (PaaS): the provider supplies the operating system, runtime and development tools, so the school manages only its own web app and data. Option (c) is Software as a Service (SaaS): the provider runs the whole application and its operating system, and staff simply use it in a browser.
sampleAnswers.feedback: All three options are matched to the correct category, and the operating system responsibility is stated and explained for each, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Option (a) is IaaS because the school rents servers. Option (c) is SaaS because it is an application that staff use in a browser.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the categories of two options, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain who manages the operating system for options (a) and (c).

sampleAnswers.answer: Cloud services let schools use computers over the internet instead of buying them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement about cloud services, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify the category of one or two options.

prompts.question: Evaluate whether the school should move its timetabling service from its own server to Software as a Service (SaaS), considering cost, control of its data and reliance on one provider.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the school already runs its student web app on a platform provided by a cloud vendor. Its timetabling service runs on a school-owned server that is ageing and needs a technician's time each term. A vendor offers the timetabling service as a subscription product, billed each year.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates the move to SaaS, weighing cost, support and data control against dependence on one provider, and reaches a reasoned judgement with its conditions
5 marks: Evaluates the move with clear links to cost, data control and reliance, with a judgement
4 marks: Explains the benefits and risks of SaaS for the school, with relevant links to its needs
3 marks: Explains one benefit or risk of SaaS for the school, with some reference to its timetabling needs
2 marks: Identifies a feature of SaaS for the school
1 mark: Makes a general statement about cloud services
markerNotes: Weigh cost, support and control of data for the school, then test each against the risk of relying on one provider.
Link each point to the school's situation, such as the ageing server or the technician's time, rather than general claims about cloud services.
A judgement that names the conditions for the move, such as data export rights, shows the evaluation is reasoned.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the benefits and risks of SaaS without reaching a judgement on whether the school should move.
Claiming that SaaS is always cheaper, without comparing it with the cost of the ageing server.
Treating control of data as unaffected by moving to a provider, when the school loses direct control over where its data is stored.

sampleAnswers.answer: Moving the timetabling service to Software as a Service (SaaS) is worthwhile if the school can manage the risks, but the decision should be weighed against control and dependence. In favour, the provider handles updates, security patches, backups and server maintenance, so the IT team can spend time supporting classrooms rather than maintaining an ageing server. A subscription also turns an uncertain repair bill into a predictable annual cost, and staff can use the service from any browser. These are real benefits of cloud computing services for a school with limited technical staff. The concerns are more serious. The school loses direct control over the software and over where its timetable data is stored, so it must check the provider's privacy and data-handling terms. Reliance on one provider also means that an outage or price rise affects every timetable user at once. The school should therefore move only with a contract that guarantees data export, service levels and a plan for changing provider. With those conditions, SaaS is the better option, but without them the school should keep its server and review the decision later.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Weighs cost and support against control of data and reliance on one provider, and gives a judgement tied to named conditions, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Moving to SaaS would remove the technician's time spent on the ageing server, and the provider would handle updates and backups. However, the school would lose some control over its data and would depend on one provider for the timetabling service. The school should think about these risks before deciding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the benefit of removing server upkeep and the risks of control and dependence, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, evaluate the move with clear links to cost, data control and reliance, and reach a judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: SaaS is a cloud service that runs in a browser, so staff can use it from any device.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a feature of SaaS, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain how browser access changes the school's cost, control or reliance on the provider.

dotPoints.description: Compare different types of cloud-based data storage in terms of access and services (public cloud; private cloud; hybrid cloud; non-cloud on premises)

prompts.question: Describe how staff access client files held in a public cloud service, and name one service that the cloud provider manages for the firm.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a four-person bookkeeping firm keeps its client files in a public cloud data storage service. Staff work from the office and from home, and the firm pays a monthly fee based on how much storage it uses.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how staff reach the client files over the internet from authorised devices, and names a provider-managed service, with both points linked to the firm
2 marks: Describes how staff access the files, OR names one provider-managed service
1 mark: Makes one accurate general statement about public cloud data storage
markerNotes: Cover both halves of the question: the access method and one named service that the provider handles.
Access needs to be specific, such as logging in over the internet from an office or home device, not just that staff use the cloud.
Name a service the provider manages, such as backup, security updates or hardware maintenance, rather than a general benefit such as lower cost.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the firm's own servers or local drives instead of the public cloud service.
Giving a general benefit, such as that it is cheaper, as the service the provider manages.
Writing that staff log in without saying the files are reached over the internet.

sampleAnswers.answer: Staff access client files over the internet from any authorised device, such as an office computer or a home laptop, by logging in to the public cloud data storage service. The cloud provider manages the underlying hardware and provides services such as automatic backup and security updates, so the firm does not need its own servers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes access over the internet from authorised devices and names provider-managed services, such as backup and security updates, with both linked to the firm, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Staff can open the firm's files from home or the office over the internet. The firm does not need to buy its own hardware.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes how staff access the files, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, name one service the provider manages, such as automatic backup, linked to the firm.

sampleAnswers.answer: The files are stored off-site in the cloud.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes an accurate general statement about cloud storage, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe how staff access the files or name one provider-managed service.

prompts.question: Compare private cloud and non-cloud on premises storage for the council's planning records, in terms of who can access the data and which services the council must manage itself.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional council stores confidential planning records and must choose between a private cloud service run by an external company and a non-cloud on premises server in its own depot. Council staff in several offices across the region need access to the same records.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Compares private cloud and on premises storage on both access and services, with accurate, linked points on who manages the hardware, backups and security
4 marks: Compares the two options accurately on access and services, with one point developed in detail
3 marks: Compares the two options on either access or services, with accurate but brief points
2 marks: Describes features of one or both options
1 mark: Makes one accurate general statement about cloud or on premises data storage
markerNotes: A comparison needs both options in each point, such as the private cloud letting staff reach the records remotely, whereas the on premises server is reached through the council's own network.
On services, say who maintains the hardware, backups and security under each option, and tie this to the council's need for control of confidential records.
Accurate brief points can earn 3 marks, but the top rows need at least one point developed in detail.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each option separately with no comparison words, so the answer is two descriptions in sequence.
Calling a private cloud a public cloud, or treating all cloud storage as the same.
Claiming on premises storage is always more secure, without explaining why this applies to these records.

sampleAnswers.answer: Private cloud and non-cloud on premises storage both serve one organisation, but they differ in access and services. A private cloud is hosted by an external company for the council alone, so staff in every office can reach the planning records over the internet or a secure link, and the provider runs the hardware, backups and updates. A non-cloud on premises server sits in the council's depot, so access depends on the council's own network and any remote connections the council sets up and secures. The council must maintain the hardware, software, backups and security itself, which gives direct control of the data storage but needs skilled staff. The private cloud suits wide access with less maintenance, while the on premises server suits full control, so the choice depends on the council's priorities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares both options on access and services, with linked points on who manages the hardware, backups and security, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A private cloud lets staff in every office reach the records over the internet, while an on premises server can only be reached through the council's own network.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the two options on access accurately, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, develop one point in detail, such as who manages the hardware, backups and security under each option.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both options store the council's records on servers, but in different places.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes one accurate general statement about storage, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe features of one or both options.

dotPoints.description: Describe key components of an organisation’s information technology infrastructure (networking, including servers, storage and end-point devices; on-premises computing; cloud computing)

prompts.question: Describe three key components of a small clinic's information technology infrastructure, giving one example each of networking, servers and end-point devices.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a small medical clinic runs its appointment booking system on-premises, on a server in the reception room, and hosts its public website through cloud computing. The practice manager is documenting the clinic's information technology infrastructure before an equipment upgrade.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes three components, each with a specific accurate example, and places on-premises and cloud computing correctly
3 marks: Describes three components with accurate examples, with the on-premises or cloud computing link stated
2 marks: Describes two components accurately, OR names three components
1 mark: Names one relevant component of the infrastructure
markerNotes: Give one concrete example for each named component, such as a router and switches for networking, rather than only the category name.
The scenario tests the on-premises and cloud split: say which parts sit in the clinic's building and which are hosted by a provider.
Describe what each component does for the clinic, not only what it is called.
commonStudentErrors: Listing components without describing them, such as servers, storage and networking.
Calling the reception server an end-point device, which confuses the central machine with the devices staff use.
Describing cloud computing as storage drives inside the clinic, when the website is hosted by a provider.

sampleAnswers.answer: The clinic's information technology infrastructure is made up of several connected components. Networking equipment, such as a router and network switches, links every computer, printer and phone so they can share data. The server in reception runs the booking system through on-premises computing, storing patient bookings on the clinic's own storage drives, while the public website runs through cloud computing and is maintained by a provider. End-point devices, such as the reception desktop and the doctors' laptops and tablets, are the devices staff use to enter and view bookings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Three components are described with specific examples, and the on-premises and cloud split is placed correctly, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The clinic has a router and switches that connect its computers. Staff use laptops and tablets to enter bookings, which are end-point devices.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes networking and end-point devices with examples, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe a third component, the server, with an example and the on-premises or cloud link.

sampleAnswers.answer: The clinic has a server.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names one component, the server, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe two components accurately.

prompts.question: Analyse how the clinic's decision to keep its booking system on-premises, while hosting its website through cloud computing, affects its control, costs and reliance on its internet connection.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a small medical clinic runs its appointment booking system on-premises, on a server in the reception room, and hosts its public website through cloud computing. The clinic has a single internet connection and a limited technology budget.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how on-premises and cloud computing change control, cost and reliability for the clinic, linking each effect to its single internet connection and limited budget
4 marks: Analyses two effects of the split arrangement accurately, with one effect linked to the internet connection or budget
3 marks: Explains one effect of on-premises or cloud computing on the clinic, with some analysis of the trade-off
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the infrastructure, with a basic statement of its effect on the clinic
1 mark: Makes one accurate general statement about on-premises or cloud computing
markerNotes: Analyse by separating the trade-off: local control and resilience for bookings against the cost and dependence of the cloud-hosted website.
Use the scenario details, the single internet connection and the limited budget, as evidence in the reasoning rather than only naming them.
A strong answer shows how the two arrangements interact, such as a connection failure affecting remote access and the website at the same time.
commonStudentErrors: Defining on-premises and cloud computing without analysing the clinic's control, costs or reliability.
Stating that cloud computing is always cheaper or more reliable, without reference to the clinic's situation.
Ignoring the single internet connection, which is the main reliability point in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Using on-premises computing for the booking system gives the clinic direct control over its information technology infrastructure. The server in reception holds appointment data within the building, so bookings can still be made if the internet connection drops, but the clinic must buy, maintain and back up its own servers, which adds cost and workload. Cloud computing for the website shifts hosting to a monthly fee and keeps the site available without local hardware, but the public site then depends on the provider's service. Because the clinic has only one internet connection, a failure would also stop the website and any remote access to the booking system at the same time. The split therefore gives local resilience for bookings and lower hosting costs for the website, but it also means the clinic must manage two different sets of risks.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses control, cost and resilience of the two arrangements, linking the single internet connection to both, and reaches a balanced conclusion, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Keeping the booking server on-premises means the clinic controls its own data, but it must pay for hardware and maintenance. Cloud hosting for the website reduces the hardware the clinic has to buy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains control and cost for the on-premises server, with a brief note on the cloud website, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, analyse two effects, with one linked to the internet connection.

sampleAnswers.answer: On-premises computing keeps the clinic's data in its own building.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes one accurate general statement about on-premises computing, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify a feature of the infrastructure and its effect on the clinic.

dotPoints.description: Describe how transmission media is used in networks

prompts.question: Classify twisted-pair cable, fibre-optic cable and wi-fi as guided or unguided transmission media, and give one typical use of each in a network.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a school is designing the network for its library, which has desktop computers in one room and wireless access for laptops and tablets. A second building 150 metres away must also be connected to the library network.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies all three media as guided or unguided; Describes a specific network use for each
2 marks: Classifies all three media as guided or unguided OR Describes a network use for two of the media
1 mark: Classifies one or two media as guided or unguided
markerNotes: Classify by how the signal travels: guided media carry signals along a physical cable or fibre, and unguided media send them through the air.
Match each use to the medium's strengths, such as twisted-pair cable for desktop connections within a room, rather than naming the medium again.
commonStudentErrors: Classifying wi-fi as guided because the laptops connect to a router by a cable.
Calling fibre-optic cable unguided because it carries light rather than electrical signals, when the light travels inside the fibre.
Giving a use that applies to every medium, such as used for the internet, instead of a use specific to each one.

sampleAnswers.answer: Twisted-pair cable and fibre-optic cable are both guided transmission media, because the signal travels along a physical cable, while wi-fi is an unguided medium that sends data through the air as radio waves. Twisted-pair cable connects the library's desktop computers to a switch, fibre-optic cable carries data over the longer link to the second building, and wi-fi serves the laptops and tablets that move around the library.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all three media as guided or unguided and describes a specific network use for each, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Twisted-pair cable and fibre-optic cable are guided media, and wi-fi is unguided. Twisted-pair cable is used in networks, and wi-fi suits laptops and tablets.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all three media as guided or unguided and describes a network use for two of them, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe a specific use for each medium, including fibre-optic cable.

sampleAnswers.answer: Twisted-pair cable is a guided medium because it is a cable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies one medium as guided or unguided, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, classify all three media, or describe a network use for two of them.

prompts.question: Explain why fibre-optic cable is better suited than twisted-pair cable to the 150-metre link between the school's two buildings, referring to signal loss and interference.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the school's main building and its science block are 150 metres apart, and the IT technician must connect their two networks. The cable route runs beside a room of heavy electrical equipment, and the technician can choose either fibre-optic cable or twisted-pair cable.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains why fibre-optic cable suits the 150-metre link, referring to signal loss and interference, and contrasts twisted-pair cable
4 marks: Explains why fibre-optic cable suits the link, referring to signal loss or interference, and contrasts twisted-pair cable
3 marks: Explains ONE advantage of fibre-optic cable for the link
2 marks: Identifies a difference between fibre-optic and twisted-pair cable
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Explain the mechanism, not only the advantage: light pulses lose less strength over distance, and fibre is not affected by electromagnetic interference.
Use the scenario values, the 150-metre distance and the electrical equipment beside the route, because these are what make the choice.
A list of advantages that is not linked to the route is less than a full explanation.
commonStudentErrors: Saying fibre-optic cable is faster, without explaining why the signal does not weaken over 150 metres.
Claiming twisted-pair cable cannot carry a signal at all, rather than that its signal weakens and suffers interference over this distance.
Describing electromagnetic interference as a problem for fibre-optic cable as well.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fibre-optic cable is better suited to the 150-metre link because it carries data as light pulses, which lose far less signal strength over distance than the electrical signals on twisted-pair cable. Twisted-pair cable is specified for runs of up to 100 metres, so on this route the signal would weaken too far for reliable reading unless extra switches or repeaters were added. Fibre-optic cable is also immune to electromagnetic interference, so the heavy electrical equipment beside the cable route cannot distort the data travelling along it. Its drawbacks are higher installation cost and the need for specialised termination, but these are outweighed by the reliability of the link. As transmission media, fibre therefore avoids the signal loss and interference that twisted-pair cable would face on this route.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains why fibre-optic cable suits the link, referring to signal loss and interference, and contrasts twisted-pair cable, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fibre-optic cable is better for a long link because it loses less signal over distance than copper cable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains ONE advantage of fibre-optic cable for the link, referring to signal loss, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, explain why it suits the link and contrast it with twisted-pair cable.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fibre-optic cable is a faster type of cable than twisted-pair.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about fibre-optic cable, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify a difference between fibre-optic and twisted-pair cable.

dotPoints.description: Explain factors that interfere with the transmission of data across a computer and social network (distance; topography; physical barriers; environmental barriers)

prompts.question: Outline how each of distance, topography, physical barriers and environmental barriers can interfere with the wireless signal sent from the farm office to the shed.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a farm office sends sensor data by a wireless link to a machinery shed 800 metres away. The signal must pass over a low ridge and a row of tall trees, the shed has a steel-framed wall, and the area often has heavy rain storms.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines how each of the four factors interferes with the wireless signal between the office and shed
3 marks: Outlines THREE of the four factors and how each interferes with the wireless signal
2 marks: Outlines TWO factors and how each affects the wireless signal
1 mark: Identifies ONE relevant factor, with a brief effect on the signal
markerNotes: Give each factor its own sentence with its effect on the signal, rather than grouping the barriers together.
Link at least one factor to the farm's situation, such as the ridge blocking the line of sight to the shed.
Keep physical barriers (walls and trees) separate from environmental barriers (rain and weather), as the dot point does.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the ridge as a physical barrier, without explaining that it is topography that blocks the line of sight.
Saying the signal stops rather than weakens, which overstates the effect of most of these factors.
Omitting one of the four factors, most often environmental barriers.

sampleAnswers.answer: Distance interferes because the signal weakens with every extra metre, a loss called attenuation, so an 800-metre link may need a repeater. Topography interferes when the low ridge blocks the line of sight between the office and the shed, forcing the signal to be reflected or bent around the hill and so losing strength. Physical barriers, such as the steel-framed wall and the trees, absorb or reflect radio waves, reducing the signal reaching the shed. Environmental barriers, such as heavy rain storms, scatter and absorb the signal, which causes rain fade on wireless links that operate at higher frequencies.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines how each of the four factors affects the wireless signal, with a specific effect for each, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Distance weakens the signal over 800 metres, so it may not reach the shed. The ridge can block the signal between the two sites.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines TWO factors, distance and topography, each with an effect on the signal, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, outline a third factor and its effect, such as physical barriers.

sampleAnswers.answer: Heavy rain can make the wireless signal weaker.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies ONE relevant factor, rain, with a brief effect on the signal, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, outline two factors, each with its effect on the signal.

prompts.question: Interpret the three signal-strength readings to explain how distance and topography each affect the wireless link, and recommend a fix suited to the terrain.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a technician measures the wireless signal strength from the farm office at three points. At 200 metres on open ground the signal is 80 per cent of full strength, at 400 metres on open ground it is 55 per cent, and at 400 metres on the far side of the ridge it is 20 per cent.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Interprets all three readings to separate distance from topography; Recommends a fix linked to the terrain
4 marks: Interprets the readings to separate the effects of distance from topography
3 marks: Interprets the open-ground readings to show the effect of distance on signal strength
2 marks: Identifies that signal strength weakens with distance or the ridge
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about wireless signal strength
markerNotes: Interpret the numbers: compare the two open-ground readings to isolate distance, then compare the two 400-metre readings to isolate topography.
Quote the readings in the answer, such as 80 to 55 per cent, rather than saying the signal gets weaker.
The recommendation should follow from the readings: raising the antennas or adding a repeater addresses terrain, while moving the antennas further apart does not.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the three readings without interpreting what they show about distance and topography.
Attributing the 20 per cent reading to distance alone, even though it is at the same 400 metres as the 55 per cent reading.
Recommending moving the antennas further apart to fix a loss caused by the ridge.

sampleAnswers.answer: On open ground, signal strength falls from 80 per cent at 200 metres to 55 per cent at 400 metres, which shows that distance alone reduces the signal through attenuation as its energy spreads. The reading behind the ridge is much lower, at 20 per cent at the same 400 metres, so topography is the main additional cause. The ridge blocks the line of sight, so the wireless signal must be reflected or diffracted around the hill, which causes a much larger loss than distance does. The technician should therefore raise the antennas above the ridge or add a repeater on the ridge, rather than simply moving the antennas further apart, because the terrain causes most of the loss.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Interprets all three readings to separate distance from topography, and recommends a fix linked to the terrain, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The signal falls from 80 to 55 per cent between 200 and 400 metres on open ground, so distance reduces the strength. The reading behind the ridge is lower, but the numbers alone do not show how much of that is caused by the ridge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Interprets the open-ground readings to show the effect of distance on signal strength, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, interpret all three readings to separate distance from topography.

sampleAnswers.answer: Wireless signals get weaker over longer distances.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about wireless signal strength, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify that signal weakens as distance or the ridge increases.

dotPoints.description: Investigate ways to improve data flow within a system, considering proximity and modes of connectivity (size, location and power of antennae when using satellite and microwave; traffic filtering; flow scheduling and traffic monitoring on telecommunications, including wireless broadband for mobile devices (3G→), Bluetooth and wi-fi)

prompts.question: Apply traffic filtering and flow scheduling to the café's network, stating one specific improvement that each would make to data flow.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a café's wi-fi slows sharply at lunchtime, when customers stream video, and the point-of-sale tablets lose their connection. The owner's router has no traffic controls, and staff download large software updates during lunch service.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Applies traffic filtering and flow scheduling to the café's network, with a specific improvement to data flow for each; Uses traffic monitoring to check the result
3 marks: Applies both techniques to the café's network, with a specific improvement for one of them
2 marks: Applies ONE technique to the café's network, with a specific improvement to data flow
1 mark: Identifies ONE relevant technique for controlling network traffic
markerNotes: Apply each technique to the scenario: filtering for the tablets against customer video, and scheduling for the lunchtime downloads.
Say what changes for data flow, such as more bandwidth for the tablets or fewer payment delays, not only what the technique is.
Traffic monitoring is the check that shows the change worked, so mention it as a step rather than as a third improvement.
commonStudentErrors: Defining traffic filtering or flow scheduling without applying either one to the café.
Recommending a faster internet plan as the improvement for each technique, which is not what either technique does.
Suggesting flow scheduling for customer video, when scheduling moves known bulk transfers to other times.

sampleAnswers.answer: Traffic filtering would improve data flow for the tablets by giving the point-of-sale traffic priority over customer video, so payments are not delayed on the café's wi-fi. The router could cap or block streaming from customer devices during service, which frees bandwidth for the tablets. Flow scheduling would move the software updates to a quiet period, such as the hour after closing, so the large downloads no longer compete with lunchtime sales. Traffic monitoring should be used first to confirm which devices use most of the bandwidth, so the owner can check that these changes improve data flow.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Applies both techniques with a specific improvement to data flow for each, and uses traffic monitoring to check the result, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Traffic filtering would stop customer video from slowing the tablets. Flow scheduling could be used for the software updates.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Applies traffic filtering with a specific improvement to data flow, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, apply flow scheduling with a specific improvement as well.

sampleAnswers.answer: Traffic filtering is a way to control network traffic.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies traffic filtering as a relevant technique, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, apply it to the café and state a specific improvement to data flow.

prompts.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of two changes for the café's data flow: moving the wi-fi access point to a central, higher position at the counter, or giving the point-of-sale tablets a separate wireless broadband connection.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the café's wi-fi access point sits in a storeroom behind a metal shelving unit, about 12 metres from the counter where the tablets are used. Customers and staff share this one access point, and lunchtime video streaming causes most of the congestion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates both changes for the café's data flow and judges which is more effective; Qualifies the judgement for congestion and cost
5 marks: Evaluates both changes with sound reasons, and reaches a justified view
4 marks: Evaluates one change in detail, and weighs the other change briefly
3 marks: Describes both changes with some relevant effects on data flow
2 marks: Describes one change with a basic effect on data flow
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about wi-fi or wireless broadband
markerNotes: Evaluate means judge effectiveness: say which change works better for the stated problem and why, with a qualification.
Use proximity and line of sight to explain why moving the access point helps, and shared congestion to explain why it may not be enough.
Mention the cost of the broadband option and its reliance on mobile signal at the counter, so that the judgement is balanced.
commonStudentErrors: Describing both changes without judging which is more effective for data flow.
Blaming the 12-metre distance alone, when the storeroom and metal shelving also block the signal.
Claiming a separate wireless broadband connection always fixes data flow, without considering mobile signal strength at the counter.

sampleAnswers.answer: Moving the wi-fi access point to a central, higher position at the counter would address proximity, the main cause of weak signal, because the tablets currently connect through a storeroom and behind metal shelving. A clearer line of sight and a shorter path should give the tablets faster, more reliable data flow at little cost. However, the same access point would still serve every customer's phone and video stream, so congestion at lunchtime would remain. A separate wireless broadband connection gives the tablets their own path, using a different one of the modes of connectivity that avoids the shared network, but it depends on mobile signal strength at the counter and adds a monthly cost. Overall, relocating the access point is the more effective first change because it removes the cause of weak signal, while wireless broadband is worth considering only if congestion persists after the move.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates both changes for data flow, judges the access point move the more effective first step, and qualifies this for congestion and cost, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Moving the access point would help, because the tablets currently connect through a storeroom and behind metal shelving that block the signal. The wireless broadband option would give the tablets their own connection, but it adds a monthly cost.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates the access point move in detail and weighs the broadband option briefly against cost, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, evaluate both changes with sound reasons and reach a justified view.

sampleAnswers.answer: A separate wireless broadband connection could make the tablets faster.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the broadband option with a basic effect on the tablets' speed, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe both changes with their effects on data flow.

dotPoints.description: Investigate the application of graph theory and network theory in the design of optimised computer networks (adjacency; centrality; connectedness; weighted graphs)

prompts.question: Calculate the degree of device C, the total cable length of the network, and the shortest cable route from device A to device E.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a small office network has five devices, A to E, joined by these direct cables with lengths in metres: A to B 10, B to C 15, C to D 20, A to C 30 and C to E 25. No other cables exist, and each cable carries data in both directions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Calculates the degree of device C, the total cable length and the shortest route from A to E, showing working
3 marks: Calculates the degree and total cable length, showing working; Identifies the shortest route from A to E
2 marks: Calculates TWO of the three values, showing working for each
1 mark: Calculates ONE of the three values correctly
markerNotes: Show the working for each value, such as the list of cables that meet at device C, so that method marks are available even if a final figure is wrong.
The shortest route is a comparison: list the candidate routes from A to E with their totals, then choose the smaller.
Degree means the number of direct connections, so count the cables that meet at the device, not the devices further away.
commonStudentErrors: Counting device C's degree as 3 by missing one of its four cables.
Choosing A to C to E as the shortest route without comparing it with A to B to C to E.
Adding only the cables on the shortest route when the question asks for the total cable length of the whole network.

sampleAnswers.answer: The degree of device C is 4, because it is directly connected to devices A, B, D and E. The total cable length is 100 metres (10 + 15 + 20 + 30 + 25). Treating the cable lengths as weighted graphs, the shortest route from A to E is A to B to C to E, at 50 metres, which is shorter than A to C to E at 55 metres. Every device can reach every other device, so the network has connectedness.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the degree, total cable length and shortest route from A to E, showing working for each, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Device C has a degree of 4, because it is connected to A, B, D and E. The total cable length is 100 metres, found by adding all five cables.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the degree and total cable length, showing working for each, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, also identify the shortest route from A to E.

sampleAnswers.answer: Device C has four direct connections, so its degree is 4.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates the degree of device C with working, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, calculate a second value, the total cable length, showing working.

prompts.question: Examine how the central position of device C affects the network's connectedness and vulnerability to failure, and how the layout could be optimised.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: the same five-device office network has device C as its only link between devices D and E and the rest of the network. The office manager wants the office to keep working if device C fails.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Examines how device C's position affects connectedness and vulnerability to failure; Proposes a layout improvement, weighed against the weighted graph
5 marks: Examines how device C's position affects connectedness, with sound reasons; Proposes a layout change linked to the graph
4 marks: Examines how device C's position affects connectedness, with relevant reasons
3 marks: Describes device C's role as a connection point in the network
2 marks: Identifies device C as a central device in the network
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Centrality is about position: count the connections and check which routes pass through the device, not only the number of cables.
Connectedness can be tested by imagining the device removed and checking which devices can still reach each other.
Support any layout change with the weighted graph, such as the extra cable length weighed against the gain in alternative paths.
Answers could include: device C as the single link to devices D and E; device C having four direct connections
commonStudentErrors: Calling device C the most important device without showing how its connections or routes support that claim.
Saying the whole network stops working if C fails, when A and B can still reach each other.
Proposing a new cable without considering its length or the trade-off in total cable length.

sampleAnswers.answer: Device C has the highest centrality in the network: it has four connections, more than any other device, and it lies on every route between devices D and E and the rest of the network. Its position affects connectedness directly, because if device C fails, devices D and E lose their only link and the network splits into two parts. In network theory terms, device C is a single point of failure, so a designer should consider adjacency and the number of alternative routes, not only cable lengths. The weighted graph shows that the 15-metre cable from B to C forms part of the shortest route from A to E, so a faster or shorter link there would also improve performance. To optimise the layout, the designer could add a second cable from device D to device B, which keeps D connected if C fails, although E would still depend on C. That extra cable adds to the total length, a trade-off the weighted graph lets the designer quantify before deciding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Examines device C's centrality and connectedness in depth, tests the failure scenario, and weighs a layout improvement using the weighted graph, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Device C is central because it has four links, so the network depends on it. If C fails, devices D and E cannot reach the other devices, so the network is split.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Examines how device C's central position affects connectedness, linking it to devices D and E, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, propose a layout change linked to the graph.

sampleAnswers.answer: Device C has four cables, so it is an important device.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies device C as a central device with four cables, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe its role as a connection point in the network.

dotPoints.description: Explore device interoperability within an Internet of Things (IoT) based enterprise network, including supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA)

prompts.question: Describe the purpose of a SCADA system at a water treatment plant, and give two examples of the devices it connects.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional water treatment plant has pressure sensors, flow meters, pumps and valves at several sites, all monitored from a central control room. The plant's operators need to see and adjust the whole system from one place.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the purpose of SCADA accurately; Gives two examples of the devices it connects
2 marks: Describes the purpose of SCADA in general terms
1 mark: Identifies ONE relevant device of a SCADA system
markerNotes: Give the purpose as monitoring and control from one place, and name devices that are actually connected to the system.
Describe the purpose in terms of monitoring and control, not only as a data or computer system.
Answers could include: pressure sensors; flow meters; pumps; valves
commonStudentErrors: Describing SCADA as a type of computer or software without its purpose of monitoring and controlling processes.
Giving two examples of the same kind of equipment, such as two different sensors.
Naming the control room as a device that the system connects.

sampleAnswers.answer: SCADA, or supervisory control and data acquisition, monitors and controls the plant's processes from a central control room, collecting readings and sending commands to remote equipment. Two devices it connects are pressure sensors, which report pipe pressure, and pumps or valves, which operators can adjust remotely. In an Internet of Things setting, these sensors and controls share a network, so the whole plant can be seen and managed from one place.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the purpose of SCADA accurately as monitoring and control from one place, and gives two devices it connects, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: SCADA lets operators monitor the plant from one place. Pressure sensors are one of the devices it uses.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the purpose of SCADA in general terms, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe the purpose accurately and give two devices it connects.

sampleAnswers.answer: SCADA uses sensors to collect data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one relevant device, sensors, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe the purpose of SCADA in general terms.

prompts.question: Discuss the challenges of achieving device interoperability when a water utility adds IoT sensors from several manufacturers to its existing SCADA system, and whether standards or gateways would resolve them.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a water utility runs a SCADA system built over many years, with older controllers from one manufacturer. It now wants to add new IoT flow and pressure sensors from three other manufacturers, and each brand uses its own data format and communication method.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses several interoperability challenges for the SCADA system in depth; Weighs whether standards or gateways would resolve them
5 marks: Discusses at least three challenges with sound reasons, and comments on how each affects the utility's SCADA system
4 marks: Discusses two challenges with relevant reasons for the utility's SCADA system
3 marks: Describes one or two challenges of interoperability with some relevant detail
2 marks: Identifies one challenge of interoperability
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about IoT devices or SCADA systems
markerNotes: Discuss means identify the challenges and weigh them: say why each one matters to the utility, then comment on how it could be managed.
Use the scenario details, the older controllers and the three other manufacturers, to make the challenges concrete.
Security is a valid challenge here, but link it to the enterprise network and the SCADA system rather than to general internet safety.
Answers could include: different data formats; legacy controllers; security
commonStudentErrors: Listing challenges, such as different brands or cost, without reasons or effects on the SCADA system.
Stating that all IoT devices work with SCADA automatically, which is the very problem the scenario raises.
Discussing only hardware, and missing the data format and communication-method problems.

sampleAnswers.answer: Device interoperability is difficult here because the new IoT sensors and the older SCADA controllers may use different data formats, so a reading from one brand cannot be understood by another without translation. The older controllers may use communication methods that newer Internet of Things devices do not support, which requires gateways or protocol converters that add cost and points of failure. The utility must also ensure that data from every device reaches the supervisory control and data acquisition system reliably and at consistent intervals across the enterprise network, or operators may act on out-of-date readings during an emergency. Security is a further challenge, since each new connected device extends the attack surface of the enterprise network and must be secured to the same standard as the SCADA system. Standards-based protocols and a documented integration plan would reduce these challenges, but each device should be tested before full connection.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses several interoperability challenges in depth, including data formats, legacy controllers and security, and weighs how standards and gateways would help, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Different data formats mean readings from the new sensors cannot be read by the older controllers without translation. The new sensors may also need gateways to connect, which adds cost and a point of failure.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses two challenges, data formats and the need for gateways, with reasons, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, discuss at least three challenges and comment on how each affects the SCADA system.

sampleAnswers.answer: The new sensors may use a different data format from the controllers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one challenge, different data formats, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe a challenge with some relevant detail.

dotPoints.description: Investigate communication protocols between devices in an Internet of Things (IoT) network

prompts.question: Classify each of the following IoT communication technologies as short-range or long-range, giving one reason for each: Bluetooth Low Energy, Zigbee, wi-fi and LoRaWAN.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a city council is planning an Internet of Things network of sensors across a park, its depot and a nearby suburb. It is comparing four communication technologies before choosing the ones for each site.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Classifies each of the four technologies as short-range or long-range, with a specific reason for each based on range or power use
3 marks: Classifies all four technologies correctly, with a reason for three of them
2 marks: Classifies two or three technologies correctly, with a reason for each
1 mark: Classifies ONE technology correctly
markerNotes: Classify by range first: short-range technologies cover a building or a small area, and long-range technologies cover kilometres.
Give a reason based on a property such as range, power use or mesh relaying, not on the technology's name or popularity.
commonStudentErrors: Classifying wi-fi as long-range because it connects to the internet.
Calling LoRaWAN short-range because it is a wireless technology.
Giving a reason that does not describe the technology, such as that it is popular.

sampleAnswers.answer: These communication protocols split into two groups by range. Bluetooth Low Energy is short-range, reaching only tens of metres, and is designed to use very little power for wearable and sensor devices. Zigbee is also short-range, forming a low-power mesh in which each device relays data to its neighbours, which suits sensors within one building or park. Wi-fi is short-range in this sense, covering a building or a small area, and uses more power than the other two, so it suits devices with a mains supply. LoRaWAN is long-range, reaching kilometres with very low data rates, so it suits Internet of Things sensors spread across a whole suburb.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all four technologies correctly, each with a reason based on range or power use, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bluetooth Low Energy and Zigbee are short-range because they cover only small areas. LoRaWAN is long-range because it covers large distances.
