Naming the hardware is not enough; state what analysts can now do that they could not do before.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a history of computer hardware, such as early mainframes, instead of the impact on analytics.
Naming CPUs and GPUs as the impact itself, without stating what changed for analysts.
Claiming faster processors make data cleaning or quality checks unnecessary.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Outlines two distinct impacts of improved processing power on data analytics, each linked to what analysts can do
1 mark: Outlines ONE impact of improved processing power on data analytics

sampleAnswers.answer: Greater processing power from multi-core CPUs and GPUs has improved data analytics by letting analysts query large datasets faster. It also makes computationally intensive machine learning practical, because GPUs run many calculations in parallel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines two distinct impacts, faster querying of large datasets and practical machine learning, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Computers today are much faster than they used to be, which is why analysts use GPUs. This means that analysis is quicker.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines ONE impact, quicker analysis, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, outline a second distinct impact, such as handling larger datasets or running machine learning.

prompts.question: Investigate how advancements in BOTH storage/memory and communication media have enabled modern cloud-based data analytics.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional logistics company stores several years of delivery and vehicle sensor data in a cloud service such as Google BigQuery or Amazon S3. Its analysts work from several offices and query the same data each week.
markerNotes: The stem asks for both storage/memory and communication media; an answer that covers one area only cannot reach the middle bands.
Show the link: cheap storage made large datasets practical to keep, and fast networks made it practical to move them to the cloud for analysis.
Use the logistics scenario to show a concrete consequence, such as analysts in several offices querying the same warehouse.
Answers could include: cheap high-capacity cloud storage; solid-state drives; larger RAM; high-bandwidth fibre networks
commonStudentErrors: Covering only storage, or only networks, although the question asks for both.
Listing specifications such as 'SSDs are fast' without saying how they enabled cloud analytics.
Treating storage (keeping data) and memory (RAM used during processing) as the same thing.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Investigates specific advances in storage and in communication media, and how they work together to enable cloud analytics for the logistics company
3 marks: Explains how advances in both storage and communication media enabled cloud analytics, with a clear link between them
2 marks: Describes one advance in storage or communication media and how it enabled cloud analytics
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about storage, communication or cloud analytics

sampleAnswers.answer: Advances in storage and memory have made cloud-based data analytics economically feasible. Cheap, high-capacity cloud storage, together with solid-state drives in data centres, lets enterprises keep big data sets and historical records on hand, while larger RAM allows analytics engines to hold working datasets in memory for rapid querying. Advances in communication media have made these remote resources practical to use. High-bandwidth fibre networks allow the logistics company's sensor and delivery data to reach a data warehouse in the cloud and be queried by analysts in several offices. Without this bandwidth, cheap storage would be negated by slow transfers, so the two advances work together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Investigates the storage and RAM advances and the high-bandwidth fibre networks, showing how they work together for the logistics company, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cheap cloud object storage means a logistics company can keep several years of delivery records in one place and analyse them without buying its own servers. Better internet connections also help with cloud analytics.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one storage advance and how it enabled cloud analytics, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain a specific advance in communication media and link it to the storage advance.

sampleAnswers.answer: Modern computers have better storage and faster internet, which makes data analytics better in the cloud. Cloud services like Google BigQuery are popular for businesses.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about better storage and faster internet, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe one storage advance and how it enabled cloud analytics.

prompts.question: Explain how the advancement of hardware can affect the processing of data from the data warehouse for this coffee shop chain.
markerNotes: The top answer explains how each hardware advance changes the processing of this chain’s warehouse data, for example faster processors analyse data sooner and more memory stores more branch data.
A 2-mark answer identifies advances, such as faster processors or better storage, but does not explain how they affect the chain’s processing.
Answers that also refer to communication media, such as fibre optics for the cloud warehouse, cover the full range of hardware the scenario points to.
commonStudentErrors: Names advances such as faster processors without saying how they affect processing this chain’s data.
Describes what a data warehouse is rather than the hardware advance that affects it.
Writes about software or the user interface instead of hardware.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains how the advancement of hardware can affect the processing of data from the data warehouse for the coffee shop chain
2 marks: Outlines how the advancement of hardware can affect the processing of data from the data warehouse for the coffee shop chain OR Identifies advancements in hardware that can affect the processing of data from the data warehouse
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
prompts.scenario:
A coffee shop chain has branches in all major cities in Australia. It collects a large volume of sales data as well as geographic and demographic data from each of its coffee shop branches.

The chain plans to use a cloud-based data warehouse for storage and for future analysis.

sampleAnswers.answer: Advancements in hardware such as processing power can allow for the organisation to analyse data from the datawarehouse more quickly, increasing the volume and velocity at which it is processed. This would allow the organisation to discover trends and patterns more efficiently, leading to better decision making. Advancements in storage and memory can also allow for the data warehouse to store more data at a time, increasing its volume and variety of stored data, such as comparing data from multiple branches or timeframes at once. This in turn can be analysed to provide deeper insights into data, increasing the quickly at which data is processed, and allowing the coffee chain to make even better decisions and predictions. Finally, advancements in communication media involves improvements to cloud storage media, which the coffee shop chain is planning to use. This advancement would further enhance the above for a cloud storage data warehouse in securely storing and analysing data in an accessible cloud location.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how processing power lets the chain “analyse data from the datawarehouse more quickly”, and how more storage lets it “store more data at a time”. It also covers communication media for the cloud warehouse. It still earned full marks despite slips such as “datawarehouse” and “increasing the quickly at which”, because the ladder rewards the content, so students should not copy them.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The CPUs used in the data warehouse servers will allow the coffee shop chain to quickly process large amounts of sales and demographic data, enabling faster decision-making. Advancements in storage such as faster RAM and Solid-State Disk drives can provide more secure and efficient ways to store vast amounts of data.

Better communication media such as fibre optics enable quicker sharing and online processing of data, to ensure that the coffee shop chain can access the latest information from each branch in real-time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how faster CPUs let the chain “quickly process large amounts” of sales data, and how faster storage offers “more secure and efficient ways to store” data. It also links fibre optics to “real-time” access.

sampleAnswers.answer: Advancements in hardware, such as faster processors and more memory, can improve how data is processed. Better communication media such as fibre optics also help.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying advancements in hardware, faster processors, more memory and fibre optics, but not explaining how they affect the chain’s processing. To reach 3 marks, the answer must explain the effect, for example that faster processors let the chain analyse its branch data sooner.

sampleAnswers.answer: The coffee shop chain collects a large amount of sales data, so it will need powerful computers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information about the chain’s data needs, with no advancement in hardware named. To reach 2 marks, the answer must identify an advancement in hardware, such as faster processors or better storage.

prompts.question: Describe how advancements in software have empowered data analytics. In your answer, refer to the scenario.
markerNotes: The top answer describes how software advances, such as automation and real-time updating, have empowered analytics, and then refers to the scenario’s dashboard and the move away from spreadsheets.
A 2-mark answer outlines one advancement or identifies several without describing how they help analytics, and it does not need to use the scenario.
Markers should look for the reference to the scenario, because the top row requires it and the 2-mark rows do not.
commonStudentErrors: Describes dashboards in general as visual displays without naming an advancement in software.
Describes the old spreadsheet process rather than how the new software improves analytics.
Names software advances such as automation without describing their effect on analysing employee performance.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how advancements in software have empowered data analytics, with reference to the scenario
2 marks: Outlines ONE advancement in software that has empowered data analytics OR Identifies advancements in software that affect data analytics
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
prompts.scenario:

sampleAnswers.answer: Advancemets in software have empowered data analytics as by updating the system under industry 4.o, the business is able to automate processes and allow for real time feedback and analytics which, in turn provide more in depth information on the perfomance on the business, allowing them to focus on their effiecency in other key areas. Instead of using spreadhseets, and manually uploading data to track performance, wasting unnessarcy amounts of time, they use a constantly updated data dashboard that visually highlights the key information such as employee performance in each departemnt, signifying where the business needs to implememt more resources, allowing for a more efficent and well performing business.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing how automation and “real time feedback and analytics” give more in-depth information, and by referring to the scenario, “Instead of using spreadsheets” and the “constantly updated data dashboard”. It still earned full marks despite slips such as “perfomance” and “effiecency”, because the ladder rewards the content, so students should not copy them.

sampleAnswers.answer: Advancements in software have transformed data analytics by enabling faster processing of large datasets, automation, real-time insights and enhanced visualisation. In the scenario, the company moved from static spreadsheets to dynamic dashboards, which will allow users to uncover patterns and trends that might have gone undetected in the past. These dashboards enable users to drill down into a specific area of interest without requiring programming skills. They also assist in improving decision-making by presenting trends, comparisons and key performance indicators clearly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing how software advances bring “faster processing of large datasets” and automation, and by referring to the scenario, where the company “moved from static spreadsheets to dynamic dashboards”.

sampleAnswers.answer: Software that updates data automatically in real time has helped data analytics. Users can now see trends without building a new report each time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining ONE advancement, real-time updating, but without referring to the scenario. To reach 3 marks, the answer must describe how this advancement empowers analytics, for example by referring to the company’s move from spreadsheets to a dashboard.

sampleAnswers.answer: The company now shows employee performance on a dashboard rather than in spreadsheets.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving some relevant information from the scenario, but no advancement in software is named. To reach 2 marks, the answer must name an advancement in software that affects data analytics, such as real-time updating or automation.

scenarioImage.alt: The employee performance dashboard: a bar chart by department, a monthly productivity line graph, an attendance heat map and a table of the highest performing employees

dotPoints.description: Describe online analytical processing (OLAP)

prompts.question: State the primary function of an OLAP system.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a retail chain's business manager wants to explore three years of sales data by product, region and month, changing the view on screen without waiting for a new report.
markerNotes: The primary function is fast, interactive, multidimensional analysis, as distinct from recording individual transactions, which is the role of OLTP systems.
A short answer suits STATE, but it must include the multidimensional element; 'it analyses data' is too general.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that OLAP records or stores transactions, which describes transaction processing rather than analysis.
Writing 'OLAP is for analysis' without saying what kind of analysis, such as multidimensional or interactive.
Confusing OLAP with a chart type or a spreadsheet, rather than a system for querying data.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: States the primary function of OLAP as fast, interactive, multidimensional analysis of large data volumes
1 mark: States a general function of OLAP

sampleAnswers.answer: The primary function of OLAP, or online analytical processing, is to allow fast, interactive, multidimensional analysis of large sales data, such as viewing sales by product, region and month, typically held in a data warehouse.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the primary function accurately, as fast, interactive, multidimensional analysis, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: An OLAP system is used to analyse data, which helps managers make decisions about their business.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States a general function, analysing data, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, state the multidimensional and interactive element of OLAP.

prompts.question: Describe how an OLAP cube would allow a retail manager to analyse sales data. Use the dimensions of 'Product', 'Time', and 'Location' in your answer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a national retail chain's regional manager needs to understand sales performance in detail. The sales data is organised by product, time and store location, and the manager wants answers without writing database queries.
markerNotes: Define each operation in one clause, then give an example using the named dimensions, such as slicing on Product or drilling from year to quarter on Time.
Describe the cube as storing pre-calculated summaries across its dimensions, and say why this makes responses quick for the manager.
Use the three named dimensions throughout; an answer that omits one of them loses the 'use the dimensions' requirement.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the cube as a 3D chart or graphic, rather than a data structure for multidimensional analysis.
Confusing slice and dice, for example by describing a dice as selecting one product.
Describing drill down as zooming in on a chart, rather than moving to a lower level of a dimension such as from year to month.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes how the Product, Time and Location dimensions let the manager slice, dice and drill down, each with a retail example
3 marks: Describes the cube's dimensions and at least two operations, with an example of one
2 marks: Describes the cube as organising sales by Product, Time and Location, with one way the manager could analyse it
1 mark: States that an OLAP cube stores sales data or is a multidimensional structure

sampleAnswers.answer: An OLAP cube would pre-calculate and store sales data across the dimensions of Product, Time, and Location. This allows the retail manager to perform multi-dimensional analysis with near-instantaneous results. For example, they could 'slice' the cube to view total sales for a single 'Product' across all times and locations. They could 'dice' the cube to look at a very specific intersection, like sales of 'Laptops' in 'Sydney' during 'December'. They could also 'drill down' on the 'Time' dimension to move from viewing total annual sales to breaking it down by quarter, month, and then day, all without writing complex database queries.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes slice, dice and drill down on the Product, Time and Location dimensions, each with a retail example, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: An OLAP cube organises sales by Product, Time and Location, so the manager can look at the sales data in different ways. For example, they could look at the sales for one product across all locations.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the cube as organising sales by Product, Time and Location, with one way to analyse it, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe at least two operations, such as slice and drill down, with an example.

sampleAnswers.answer: An OLAP cube is a special type of database that stores sales data. It is useful because it is faster than other databases.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States that the cube is a database that stores sales data, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe the cube as organising sales by Product, Time and Location.

dotPoints.description: Assess data integrity in the development of a data visualisation (ownership; source; validation; risk)

prompts.question: Distinguish between a data source and data validation in the context of data integrity.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a small team is preparing a dataset of school attendance figures, supplied as a spreadsheet by a school, for a public dashboard. Before the dashboard goes live, the team must confirm that the data can be trusted.
markerNotes: Define the source as origin and ownership, and validation as a checking process applied to the data, then state the difference.
Validation is an activity performed on the data, while the source is a fact about where it came from; the contrast is what earns the second mark.
Linking both terms to integrity, meaning accuracy and trustworthiness, strengthens the answer without adding length.
Answers could include: checks for accuracy; completeness; consistency
commonStudentErrors: Defining data validation as 'where the data came from' or as 'who owns the data'.
Treating source and validation as synonyms, both meaning 'checking the data'.
Describing data integrity as 'having a lot of data' rather than the accuracy and trustworthiness of the data.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Distinguishes a data source, as where the data came from, from data validation, as checking accuracy and completeness
1 mark: Defines ONE term accurately

sampleAnswers.answer: A data source is where the data comes from, including its ownership. Data validation is the process of checking the accuracy and completeness of the data before a data visualisation is built, protecting data integrity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Distinguishes a data source as the origin of the data from validation as a checking process, linked to integrity, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data source is a place where data comes from, such as a spreadsheet or a website. Data validation is also about the data and helps make sure it is good.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines a data source accurately, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, define data validation as a check of the data's accuracy, completeness and consistency.

prompts.question: Assess the risk to an enterprise that creates a public-facing data visualisation based on data from an unverified third-party source.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a consumer goods company downloads a dataset from an unfamiliar website showing rapid growth in its product category, and places a chart based on it on its public website and in marketing materials. Nobody on the team has checked who produced the dataset or how it was collected.
markerNotes: Assess means judge the size of the risk: link the unverified source to the visualisation's integrity, then to consequences for the company, then judge how serious it is.
Name the consequence, such as customers relying on wrong figures, reputational damage, or a complaint about copyright or terms of use, rather than saying 'bad things could happen'.
A reasoned judgement, such as 'the risk is high because errors cannot be corrected once the chart is published', is needed for the upper bands.
commonStudentErrors: Listing risks without judging how serious they are, which describes rather than assesses.
Assuming the data is wrong because it came from the internet, rather than saying its accuracy is unknown because it is unverified.
Writing only about the cost of the campaign, not about public and reputational consequences.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Assesses the risk of an unverified source to the enterprise, linking it to reputation and decisions, with a judgement of how serious it is
3 marks: Explains the main risks to data integrity and to the company's reputation
2 marks: Identifies one or two relevant risks, including inaccurate data or reputational damage
1 mark: States a risk in general terms

sampleAnswers.answer: The overall risk to the enterprise is high. Because the third-party source is unverified, the data integrity of the data visualisation is unknown, and the figures may be inaccurate, biased or outdated. Without data validation, no one can show that the chart is accurate, and the unknown ownership of the dataset means its copyright status is also unclear. Publishing the chart risks misleading customers, causing reputational damage and a loss of trust. Decisions based on it could also lead to financial losses. The risk is high because a published error spreads quickly and cannot be recalled from every audience.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses the risk by linking the unknown integrity to reputational harm and loss of trust, and judges the risk high with a reason, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Using unverified data could mean the chart is wrong, and customers may stop trusting the company. This could hurt the business.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two relevant risks, inaccurate data and loss of trust, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain why an unverified source makes the data unreliable and what this means for the company.

sampleAnswers.answer: There is a risk because the data came from the internet.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States a general risk, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify a specific risk, such as inaccurate data or reputational damage.

dotPoints.description: Explain the impact of enterprise data warehousing on data visualisation (analysis and use of historical data trends and patterns; correlation with current data; data refinement/optimisation)

prompts.question: Outline one major benefit a data warehouse provides for data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a mid-sized enterprise wants one dashboard showing data from its sales, marketing and human resources systems. The three systems store their records separately and in different formats.
markerNotes: One benefit, developed in two sentences, is the target: name it, then explain how it improves the visualisation.
'Single source of truth' is a recognised benefit, but explain what it means: consistent, integrated data from sales, marketing and HR systems.
Storing data is not a benefit in itself; the benefit lies in the integration, cleaning and consistency the warehouse provides.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the data warehouse 'stores data' without saying how this helps the visualisation.
Naming a benefit such as faster charts without explaining why the warehouse causes it.
Confusing a data warehouse with an ordinary operational database used for transactions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Outlines one major benefit of a data warehouse for visualisation, and explains why it matters for the dashboard
1 mark: Names a general benefit of a data warehouse

sampleAnswers.answer: Enterprise data warehousing integrates sales, marketing and HR records into one consistent data warehouse, including historical data. This single source of truth lets a dashboard give data visualisation that agrees across all three systems.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one major benefit, an integrated and consistent warehouse, and explains its effect on the dashboard, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data warehouse stores a lot of data in one place, which is useful for an enterprise.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names a general benefit, storing a lot of data, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, outline one benefit, such as integrating data from several systems, and explain its effect on the dashboard.

prompts.question: Explain how a data warehouse enables an enterprise to create visualisations that correlate historical data trends with current data.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a retail company wants a dashboard that compares this month's sales with the same month in each of the previous ten years, so managers can tell whether a recent rise is unusual. Its transaction records are held in an operational system designed for day-to-day processing.
markerNotes: Explain the mechanism: warehouses store integrated, time-stamped data over long periods, so one query can cover the last ten years and the current month.
Link the comparison to a decision, such as whether this month's sales are unusually high or part of a recurring seasonal pattern.
Contrast the operational system (current, transaction-focused) with the warehouse (history, analysis-focused) to show why the warehouse is used.
commonStudentErrors: Saying the warehouse 'shows the data on a graph' without explaining how historical and current data are brought together.
Describing historical data only, without showing how current data enters the visualisation.
Treating the warehouse as a visualisation tool, rather than a store of integrated data that visualisation tools connect to.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how integrated, time-stamped warehouse data lets a visualisation compare current figures with past trends, and what managers can judge
3 marks: Explains how the warehouse holds historical data alongside current data, with an example of a comparison
2 marks: Identifies that a warehouse stores historical data and that a visualisation can show it alongside current figures
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about data warehouses

sampleAnswers.answer:
Enterprise data warehousing stores integrated, time-stamped records. A data warehouse therefore keeps historical data over many years, so one query can cover ten years of sales alongside the current month.

A data visualisation tool can query the warehouse for the same month in each previous year and plot current data against those trends. The dashboard shows the correlation between this month's sales and the historical range, letting managers see whether a rise sits within the normal seasonal pattern or outside it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains integrated, time-stamped warehouse data, the comparison of past and current sales, and what managers can judge about a rise, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data warehouse stores historical sales, so a dashboard can show sales from previous years. The dashboard can also show this month's sales next to those figures, so managers can compare them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies that the warehouse stores historical sales and that the dashboard can show them beside this month's sales, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain how the warehouse's integrated, time-stamped data makes this comparison possible.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data warehouse is a large storage system that can hold a lot of data. Dashboards can then be made with the data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about data warehouses, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify that the warehouse stores historical data a visualisation can show alongside current figures.

dotPoints.description: Explain how big data affects the design and development of data visualisation (scope of visible information; types and depth of insight provided by the data)

prompts.question: Identify two design challenges that big data creates for data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a designer is building a map of national bus journeys from a transport dataset that records billions of GPS points over a year. The designer must decide what the chart will show and how it will load.
markerNotes: Name the challenge and its effect on the design: overplotting hides patterns, and slow rendering prevents interaction.
The two challenges should differ: visual clutter is a design problem and performance is a technical one.
A challenge is a problem for the designer, not a benefit of big data; 'big data gives more information' earns no credit here.
commonStudentErrors: Stating a benefit of big data, such as more insight, rather than a challenge for the designer.
Giving two wordings of the same problem, such as 'too many points' and 'the chart is cluttered'.
Naming general data problems such as bad data without linking them to big data.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct design challenges that big data creates for data visualisation
1 mark: Identifies ONE design challenge that big data creates for data visualisation

sampleAnswers.answer: Two design challenges big data creates for data visualisation are visual clutter, where millions of data points hide patterns and limit the scope of visible information, and rendering performance, as large datasets load slowly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two distinct challenges, visual clutter and rendering performance, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Big data is hard to show in a chart because there is so much of it. The chart might also be hard to read because it has too much in it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one challenge, too much data on the chart, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify a second, different challenge, such as slow rendering of millions of points.

prompts.question: Explain how visualising 'big data' can provide deeper and different types of insight compared to visualising a small dataset. Use an example in your answer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a national retailer can visualise either a survey of 200 customers or every transaction its stores recorded over three years. Managers want to know which visualisation would reveal more about their customers.
markerNotes: The stem asks for different types of insight as well as deeper insight: say what kind (such as segment-level patterns or rare events) and why only large data reveals it.
Use an example that a small dataset could not show, such as a rare product fault in one region, to make the difference concrete.
Explain the mechanism: a sample of 200 may miss a subgroup or a rare event, while the full transaction record contains enough cases to show it.
commonStudentErrors: Saying big data is simply 'more accurate' without describing the different insight it provides.
Giving an example that would work equally well for a small dataset, so it does not show what scale adds.
Writing only about data storage or collection, without the visualisation side of the question.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains that big data reveals different insights, including segment-level patterns, with an example compared with a small dataset
3 marks: Explains that big data reveals more detailed or different patterns than a small dataset, with a relevant example
2 marks: States that big data gives deeper insight than a small dataset, with an example
1 mark: Makes a general claim that more data is better

sampleAnswers.answer:
Visualising big data can reveal different types of insight that are impossible to detect in a small dataset. While a small sample might show only an average trend, a big data visualisation exposes variation and outliers with much higher confidence.

For example, visualising a survey of 200 customers might suggest that 'Product A' is popular. Visualising every transaction recorded over three years, however, can reveal a deeper insight: 'Product A' is extremely popular, but only with customers aged 18-24 in metropolitan areas. This segment-level pattern is visible only because the big data set contains enough cases in each segment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains that big data reveals a segment-level pattern that a 200-customer survey cannot show, with a specific comparison, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Big data gives more information, so visualising it shows deeper insights than a small dataset. For example, a company with millions of sales records can see more about its customers than a company with a small survey.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States that big data gives deeper insight, with a general example, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe one pattern that only the large dataset would reveal.

sampleAnswers.answer: Big data is good because there is more of it. Visualisations are useful and help people look at data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general claim that more data is better, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, state that big data gives deeper insight, with an example.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate bias in data collection, storage and analysis when developing visualisations (accuracy; audience; data source; unconscious bias)

prompts.question: Distinguish between bias from a data source and audience bias in the context of a data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a news website publishes a bar chart of how residents feel about a proposed development. The chart is based on an online poll that only visitors to the website could take, and readers bring their own views to the chart.
markerNotes: Locate each bias: data source bias sits in how the data was collected, while audience bias sits in the viewer's interpretation.
A concrete example, such as an online-only poll that misses people without internet access, shows the difference clearly.
Naming confirmation bias as an example of audience bias shows understanding of how viewers interpret charts.
commonStudentErrors: Defining audience bias as the audience being 'biased' in general, with no link to how they interpret the chart.
Attributing data source bias to the chart's colours or layout, which belong to the design rather than the data.
Describing both biases as the same thing, such as 'the chart is unfair'.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Distinguishes data source bias, a flaw in the data, from audience bias, a flaw in interpretation, with an example of each
1 mark: Describes one bias accurately, or names both biases in general terms

sampleAnswers.answer: Bias from a data source is a flaw in the data itself, such as an online-only poll missing some residents, which undermines accuracy. Audience bias is a flaw in how viewers interpret a data visualisation, such as confirmation bias.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Locates each bias, data source bias in the poll's data and audience bias in interpretation, and gives an example of each, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bias from a data source means the chart is biased. Audience bias means people can be biased when they look at the chart.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names both biases in general terms, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, say where each bias sits and give one example of each.

prompts.question: A tech company creates a data visualisation to show that its hiring process is fair. However, the data was collected via an opt-in survey sent only to current employees. Evaluate how unconscious bias and bias in the data source could lead to an inaccurate and misleading visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a technology company wants to publish a chart showing that its hiring process is fair. The chart uses responses from an opt-in survey sent only to current employees, and the analysts who designed it already expect a favourable result.
markerNotes: Evaluate means reach a judgement: here, whether the visualisation is misleading and how far the biases undermine the claim that hiring is fair.
Address both biases and how they interact: a skewed sample (data source bias) can be made to look favourable by analysts who choose metrics that match their expectations (unconscious bias).
Use the scenario's details: the opt-in design, the current-employee sample and the rejected applicants who are excluded.
Answers could include: selection bias; unconscious bias; the opt-in survey favouring satisfied respondents
commonStudentErrors: Describing unconscious bias in general without linking it to how the analysts would select or present the data in this case.
Listing both biases without evaluating how they combine to make the visualisation misleading.
Making an unsupported moral judgement that the company is 'lying' or 'unethical', rather than explaining how the visualisation becomes inaccurate.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Evaluates both sources of bias with sustained judgement, weighing whether the chart can support the fairness claim
5 marks: Evaluates both sources of bias with specific links to the scenario and a judgement
4 marks: Explains both biases and how each could distort the visualisation, with links to the scenario
3 marks: Explains one bias in relation to the scenario, showing how the visualisation could mislead
2 marks: Identifies two relevant biases, selection bias and unconscious bias
1 mark: Makes a general statement that bias can make a visualisation misleading

sampleAnswers.answer:
The data source is fundamentally biased. Because the opt-in survey was sent only to current employees, it excludes the perspectives of applicants who were rejected, which is a severe form of selection bias: the people who may have experienced unfairness are not represented at all. The opt-in survey design adds a second distortion, since employees who are content with the process are more likely to respond, so the sample is skewed towards positive views before any analysis begins.

Unconscious bias compounds this. Analysts who expect the process to be fair may not intend to mislead, but they can choose metrics that look favourable, such as diversity figures for one department, while leaving out less flattering measures such as the ratio of applicants to hires for each demographic group. Each choice seems reasonable in isolation, yet together they shape what the audience sees and reduce the accuracy of the chart.

Ultimately, this misleading visualisation presents a precise-looking picture of fairness built on an unrepresentative dataset and a selective set of metrics. Its accuracy cannot support the claim that the hiring process is fair, and publishing it would damage the company's credibility once the gaps are discovered.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates both biases with specific links to the scenario, shows how selection bias and unconscious bias combine, and reaches a judgement that the chart cannot support the fairness claim, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bias in the data source is a problem here, because the survey was only sent to current employees. This means people who applied and were rejected are not included, so the results may not show what really happened in hiring. The survey was also opt-in, so people who were happy with the process may be more likely to answer. Analysts might also be unconsciously biased and choose to show the results that look good, which could make the chart misleading.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains both biases and how each could distort the chart, with links to the scenario, which meets the 4-mark row. To reach 5 marks, add a judgement on how far the chart can be trusted.

sampleAnswers.answer: The survey was only sent to current employees, so it is biased. Unconscious bias could also affect the analysts who make the chart, so the chart might not be accurate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two relevant biases, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain how the excluded applicants or the opt-in responses would skew the figures.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate the effectiveness of software tools used to develop data visualisations (spreadsheets used to develop dashboards; presentation software used to present data analysis; business analytics services, including ‘as a service’ products; custom software solutions)

prompts.question: Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of using a spreadsheet to develop a data visualisation dashboard.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a small bakery owner wants a simple sales dashboard built from the sales records already kept in a spreadsheet. The owner has no budget for specialist software.
markerNotes: Give one of each: an advantage and a disadvantage. Two advantages, or two disadvantages, earn one mark.
Relate each point to dashboards: low cost matters for a small business, and limited interactivity matters when users want to filter the view.
A brief statement with a reason is enough; this is an identify question, not an evaluation.
commonStudentErrors: Giving two advantages, or two disadvantages, when the question asks for one of each.
Naming a spreadsheet feature, such as formulas, without saying whether it helps or hinders a dashboard.
Writing a vague point such as 'spreadsheets are good' or 'spreadsheets are hard' without a reason.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies one advantage and one disadvantage of a spreadsheet for the dashboard, each stated clearly
1 mark: Identifies ONE correct advantage or disadvantage of a spreadsheet for the dashboard

sampleAnswers.answer: Spreadsheet software is an advantage for a data visualisation dashboard because it is low-cost and familiar to a small business owner. Its disadvantage is limited interactivity, and performance slows noticeably with large datasets.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies an advantage, low cost and familiarity, and a disadvantage, limited interactivity with large datasets, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: An advantage of using spreadsheet software for data visualisation dashboards is its widespread availability and familiarity, making it an accessible and low-cost tool for basic data analysis.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one advantage, low cost and wide availability, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify one disadvantage of spreadsheets for the dashboard, such as limited interactivity.

prompts.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of using a business analytics service (e.g., Power BI, Tableau) compared to a custom software solution for a large enterprise's data visualisation needs.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a large bank must give its financial analysts secure, complex visualisations of trading and risk data. It is choosing between subscribing to a business analytics service, such as Power BI or Tableau, and commissioning a custom software solution built for its own systems.
markerNotes: Evaluate needs a judgement: weigh the trade-offs for a bank with secure, specialised needs and say which option is more effective and why.
Use the bank's requirements, such as security, complexity and specialised visualisations, as the criteria, and test each option against them.
Name concrete characteristics: rapid deployment and out-of-the-box dashboards for the service; integration and control over security for the custom solution.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Power BI or Tableau features without comparing them with custom software.
Assuming a custom solution is always better, without considering its higher cost, development time or maintenance.
Giving a judgement that is not connected to the bank's requirements, such as 'custom software is better' with no reason.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Evaluates both options against the bank's needs, weighing speed, cost and customisation, and reaches a reasoned judgement
4 marks: Evaluates both options, with strengths and limitations linked to the bank's needs
3 marks: Explains the strengths and limitations of both options in relation to the bank
2 marks: Describes one option's strengths or limitations with some relevance to the bank
1 mark: Makes a general statement about analytics services or custom software

sampleAnswers.answer:
Business analytics services such as Power BI or Tableau are highly effective for rapid deployment. Their out-of-the-box dashboards let the bank build and share visualisations quickly at a lower upfront cost. However, they offer limited customisation and may not meet every stringent data security protocol the bank requires.

Custom software solutions are less effective on speed and initial cost, because they need significant investment in development time and resources. Their primary strength is customisation: the visualisations can be integrated with proprietary trading and risk systems, can enforce the bank's own data governance rules, and can provide data security controls that an off-the-shelf product cannot.

For a large bank with complex and specific requirements, the custom solution is more effective overall, despite its higher cost, because it gives analysts a secure and precisely aligned tool.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates both options against the bank's needs, weighing speed, cost and customisation, and reaches a reasoned judgement that the custom solution is more effective, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A business analytics service like Power BI is quick to set up and has many features, so it would suit the bank. However, it might not do everything the bank wants. A custom software solution would be more expensive, but it could be designed for the bank's needs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the strengths and limitations of both options in relation to the bank, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, weigh the two options against the bank's security and speed needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: Custom software is made just for one company, so it is special. Power BI is a program that people can subscribe to.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement about each option, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe one option's strengths or limitations with relevance to the bank.

dotPoints.description: Interrogate data from a data visualisation (interpreting what you see; aggregation; filtering; the effect of outliers; reasoning)

prompts.question: Distinguish between aggregation and filtering in a data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional sales manager is using an interactive dashboard that shows monthly sales for every store in the company. She wants the total for each region, and then wants to look only at one product line.
markerNotes: Define each by its effect: aggregation reduces many values to one summary, while filtering shows fewer records but keeps each value as recorded.
A concrete example from the dashboard, such as total sales for a region against sales for one product line, makes the difference clear.
commonStudentErrors: Saying filtering and aggregation both 'summarise the data', without showing that filtering keeps the individual records.
Describing aggregation as 'removing data', which describes filtering.
Defining filtering as sorting the data into order.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Distinguishes aggregation, which combines values into a summary, from filtering, which selects a subset of records, with an example
1 mark: Defines ONE of the two terms accurately

sampleAnswers.answer: Aggregation combines many values into one summary, such as a regional total. Filtering selects a subset of records, leaving each value unchanged. Both let users interrogate data in an interactive dashboard, a form of data visualisation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines aggregation as a summary of many values and filtering as selecting a subset of records, with a regional total example, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aggregation is when you add up sales data to get totals. Filtering is when you use the dashboard to look at the data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines aggregation accurately, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, define filtering as selecting a subset of records, such as one product line.

prompts.question: A bar chart shows the average monthly rainfall. One month is an extreme outlier, with a value five times higher than any other. Explain the effect of this outlier on the visualisation and the reasoning process of the viewer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a viewer is looking at a bar chart of average monthly rainfall for a coastal region, to understand its typical climate before planning a holiday. One month's bar is far taller than the rest because of an exceptional storm, and the viewer has not yet noticed it.
markerNotes: Answer both parts: the visual effect on the chart (the scale and the compressed bars) and the effect on the viewer's reasoning (a misleading conclusion about typical rainfall).
Set out the reasoning steps: noticing the tallest bar, assuming it is typical, then checking whether it is an exceptional event such as a storm.
A strong answer suggests what would help, such as a note on the chart, a median, or excluding the month.
commonStudentErrors: Calling the outlier 'wrong data' or 'a mistake' without evidence; the question is about its effect on the visualisation.
Explaining only the visual effect, without describing how the viewer's conclusion would change.
Claiming the outlier changes the values of the other months' bars, when it affects only its own month's bar and the scale.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how the outlier stretches the scale and misleads the viewer's reasoning, and sets out how the viewer should check the chart
3 marks: Explains the outlier's effect on the scale and the readability of other bars, with how this could mislead the viewer
2 marks: States that the outlier makes the other bars harder to read, or that the viewer might misunderstand the climate
1 mark: Makes a general statement that outliers can affect charts

sampleAnswers.answer: The extreme outlier distorts the scale of the bar chart. The bar for that month is so tall that the axis stretches to accommodate it, flattening the other bars and making subtle differences between months hard to see. This affects the viewer's reasoning. A superficial look might lead to the incorrect conclusion that the region is extremely wet. Interpreting data carefully requires the viewer to reason that the spike is an exceptional storm, not a typical value, and to check the axis or mentally set the month aside, or use filtering tools to exclude it, before judging the typical rainfall.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how the outlier stretches the scale and misleads the viewer's reasoning, and sets out the steps the viewer should take to check it, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The outlier makes the bar chart's scale much bigger, so the other bars look small. This could make the viewer think the region has high rainfall all year round.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States that the outlier makes the other bars harder to read and that the viewer might misunderstand the climate, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain how the squashed bars lead to the misreading.

sampleAnswers.answer: Outliers are unusual values in a dataset, and they can make charts look strange. Viewers should be careful when they read charts with outliers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement that outliers can make charts look strange, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, state that the outlier makes the other bars harder to read.

dotPoints.description: Use graphic design tools to assist in the graphic development of a data visualisation

prompts.question: Demonstrate, by example, how two graphic design tools could improve the graphic development of the bar chart in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional theatre company has drafted a bar chart of monthly ticket sales for its annual report. The chart uses the default bright rainbow colours of a spreadsheet, has a three-dimensional effect that distorts the bar heights, has no title, and places the month labels at a slant so that they overlap. The chart will be shown to patrons and sponsors on the company's website.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates two graphic design tools, each with a clear example of how it improves the chart for its audience
3 marks: Demonstrates two graphic design tools, with an accurate example for one and a general description of the other
2 marks: Demonstrates ONE graphic design tool with an accurate example, OR Names two graphic design tools
1 mark: Names ONE graphic design tool
markerNotes: Demonstrate means show with a concrete example, such as which colours to use or which alignment setting to apply.
Each example should name the change and its effect on the chart, because the marker needs both to award the second mark.
Choose tools that are genuinely graphic design tools, such as colour palettes, alignment guides or text tools.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a tool without saying what it would change in the chart.
Suggesting changes to the data, such as removing months, rather than changes to the graphic design.
Describing a change of chart type, which is a data visualisation decision rather than a graphic design tool.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two graphic design tools can improve the bar chart. First, a colour palette tool can replace the default rainbow colours with two shades of one hue, so the strongest months stand out and the chart stays readable for patrons and sponsors. Second, an alignment guide or snap-to-grid tool can line up the bars and month labels on a common baseline, so the bar heights are not distorted and the labels no longer overlap. A text tool can then add a clear title, which completes the graphic development of the data visualisation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Demonstrates two graphic design tools, a colour palette and an alignment guide, each with a specific example and its effect on the chart, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A colour palette tool could change the bright rainbow colours to one shade of blue, so the chart is easier to read. Alignment guides are another graphic design tool.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Demonstrates ONE tool, a colour palette, with an accurate example, and names a second, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, describe how alignment guides would change the chart.

sampleAnswers.answer: A colour palette tool is a graphic design tool.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names ONE graphic design tool, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, show how the tool would change the chart.

prompts.question: Justify your choice of two graphic design tools for the council's chart, referring to the audience, the purpose of the visualisation and how the tools support accessibility.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a regional council is designing an interactive data visualisation of household water use by suburb for residents, many of whom are older and read charts on mobile phones. Staff can choose from a vector drawing program with grid, snapping and colour contrast tools; a free online chart builder with preset templates; and a photo editor that adds filters to images. The purpose of the chart is to help residents compare suburbs accurately.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies two graphic design tools with sound reasons linked to the audience, purpose and accessibility; Reaches a supported conclusion
5 marks: Justifies two tools with sound reasons linked to the audience and purpose
4 marks: Justifies at least one tool choice with sound reasons, referring to the audience or purpose
3 marks: Describes features of two tools with some reference to the audience
2 marks: Identifies one feature of a tool, linked to the audience or purpose
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about a graphic design tool
markerNotes: Justify means give reasons for the choice, and reject the alternative with reasons too, which earns the conclusion mark.
Connect each tool feature to a specific user need, such as older readers on small screens, rather than listing features.
Accessibility is strongest when it names a concrete need, such as colour vision deficiency or low contrast.
commonStudentErrors: Listing features of a tool without saying why they suit this audience.
Choosing the photo editor without explaining how its filters could distort the data.
Treating accessibility as a general good, rather than naming a specific reader need.

sampleAnswers.answer: Of the available graphic design tools, the vector drawing program is the better choice for the main chart. Its grid and snapping tools let the designer align each bar and label exactly, which matters because the chart must read clearly for an older audience on small screens. Its colour contrast tools can check that the bars remain distinguishable for readers with colour vision deficiency, which supports accessibility. Because the purpose is to help residents compare suburbs accurately, precise control of scale and labels is essential. The free online chart builder is a useful second tool for the early graphic development, since its preset templates speed up the first draft of the data visualisation. Its templates limit control over fonts and spacing, so the final layout should be finished in the drawing program. The photo editor should be rejected, because its filters and colour adjustments can distort the appearance of the data and reduce clarity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies both chosen tools and rejects the photo editor, with reasons linked to the audience, purpose and accessibility, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A vector drawing program lets the designer align bars and labels precisely, which helps readers. An online chart builder has preset templates that save time but offers less control over the layout.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes features of two tools with reference to readers, which meets the 3-mark row. To reach 4 marks, justify at least one tool choice with reasons linked to the audience or purpose.

sampleAnswers.answer: A photo editor adds filters to images.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about a photo editor, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, identify a feature of a tool linked to the audience or purpose.

dotPoints.description: Explain how user experience (UX) influences the development of effective data visualisations (relevance to the audience; audience interpretation; customisation; live analysis)

prompts.question: Explain why a data visualisation must be relevant to its intended audience.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a company is designing one dashboard of sales data for two users: its chief executive, who needs a quick view of company performance, and a data scientist who needs detailed data to test a forecasting model.
markerNotes: Explain the consequence of irrelevance: a summary that suits a CEO is useless to a data scientist, and detail that suits the data scientist overwhelms the CEO.
Refer to needs, goals and expertise as the reasons the audience matters.
A relevant example from the dashboard scenario makes the explanation specific.
commonStudentErrors: Saying relevance matters because it looks professional, rather than because it meets the audience's needs.
Writing that the audience must understand the chart, without explaining why different audiences need different detail.
Describing the CEO and the data scientist without relating their needs to the visualisation's design.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Explains why audiences differ in needs and expertise, and how a mismatch affects the user
1 mark: States that a visualisation should be relevant to its audience

sampleAnswers.answer: Relevance matters because a data visualisation must suit its audience, whose expertise and needs differ. A CEO needs a summary dashboard, while a data scientist needs detail, so one design harms the user experience for one of them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains that the CEO and data scientist need different detail, so one design harms one user, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A data visualisation should be relevant to its audience because it is important for people to get what they need from it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States that a visualisation should be relevant to its audience, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, explain why audiences differ in needs and expertise, with an example of a mismatch.

prompts.question: Explain how incorporating 'customisation' and 'live analysis' features can improve the user experience of a data visualisation dashboard.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a company is developing an interactive sales dashboard for its field team, who work across several regions and check results on laptops and phones. Team members need current figures, and each focuses on the metrics for their own territory.
markerNotes: Explain the mechanism for each feature: customisation lets users remove what is irrelevant to them, and live analysis lets them act on current data rather than an outdated report.
Name the UX gain: less time searching, more relevant information and faster decisions.
Refer to the team's context, such as territories, laptops and phones, and time-sensitive decisions, to show why the features matter for these users.
Answers could include: personalised metrics, filters and layouts; live data that updates as new records arrive
commonStudentErrors: Defining customisation as 'changing the colours', which is cosmetic rather than a change to what the user sees.
Describing live analysis as 'modern' or 'the data is shiny' without saying what it lets the user do.
Writing about the two features separately, with no comment on how they work together for the team.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how customisation and live analysis each improve UX for the field team, naming the UX gain for each
3 marks: Explains how both features improve UX, with a relevant link to the field team
2 marks: Describes one feature in some detail and its UX benefit, or both features in general terms
1 mark: Makes a general statement that customisation or live data is good

sampleAnswers.answer: Customisation improves the user experience of an interactive dashboard by giving each user control. A salesperson can filter the view to the metrics for their own territory, removing noise, so the dashboard is more efficient to use. Live analysis adds real-time data, so the team can act on current figures rather than a report that is already outdated. This supports faster decision-making in the field, where staff on phones and laptops need immediate answers. Together, the two features keep the dashboard's relevance high at the moment of use, so each user gets a better experience.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how customisation and live analysis each improve the experience for the field team, and why the two work together, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Customisation lets a salesperson change the dashboard so it shows what they need, which makes it easier to use. Live data is also useful because it updates.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both features in general terms, with a general benefit for each, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, explain how each feature improves the experience for the team.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dashboards with customisation and live analysis are better. People like modern things and they are more fun to use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement that the features are good, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe what customisation or live data lets the salesperson do.

prompts.question: Explain how the visualisations used in the data dashboard provided could affect the management team’s user experience and understanding of employee productivity.
markerNotes: The top answer links specific visuals to what management can see, such as the productivity line graph peaking in July or the attendance heat map, and explains why this helps: the visuals are easy to read for managers with different levels of data knowledge, and the real-time updates let them respond to changes.
An answer that describes one graph without saying how it affects the team's user experience or understanding of productivity sits at the 2-mark row.
The top row needs the effect on the management team, not only a description of what each graph shows.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what each graph shows, such as the bar chart of department scores, without explaining how it affects the management team's user experience.
Discussing only one visualisation, usually the line graph, when the question asks about the visualisations in the dashboard.
Confusing the heat map, which shows attendance and punctuality, with employee productivity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how the data visualisations provided could affect the management team’s user experience and understanding of employee productivity
3 marks: Describes how the data visualisations provided could affect the management team’s user experience and understanding of employee productivity
2 marks: Outlines how ONE feature of the data visualisations could affect the management team’s user experience and/or understanding of employee productivity
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
prompts.scenario:
As a result of advancements in technology, a company now presents employee performance information on a dashboard that is updated using real-time data, rather than spreadsheets. The data dashboard is shown.

Stimulus: Employee performance by department (bar chart, performance score): Sales about 78, Marketing about 85, HR about 70, IT about 90, Finance about 88.

Company employee productivity (line graph, productivity score by month): Jan 60, Feb 65, Mar 70, Apr 80, May 85, Jun 90, Jul 95, Aug 92, Sep 88, Oct 86, Nov 84, Dec 82.

Employee attendance and punctuality patterns by department (heat map, Jan–Dec, 80 to 99):

| | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sales | 98 | 90 | 85 | 94 | 97 | 84 | 94 | 81 | 95 | 98 | 98 | 99 |
| Marketing | 87 | 85 | 82 | 97 | 92 | 84 | 81 | 97 | 88 | 90 | 92 | 83 |
| HR | 93 | 84 | 97 | 99 | 92 | 91 | 82 | 80 | 93 | 88 | 88 | 83 |
| IT | 94 | 86 | 81 | 92 | 99 | 89 | 96 | 92 | 90 | 96 | 95 | 86 |
| Finance | 80 | 90 | 80 | 98 | 87 | 83 | 80 | 98 | 99 | 99 | 90 | 92 |

Highest performing employees:

| Employee | Department | Performance score | Attendance (%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alice | Sales | 78 | 95 |
| Bob | Marketing | 85 | 92 |
| Charlie | HR | 70 | 88 |
| David | IT | 90 | 97 |
| Emma | Finance | 88 | 94 |

Note: This data dashboard dynamically updates the visualisations using real-time records.

scenarioImage.alt: The employee performance dashboard: a bar chart by department, a monthly productivity line graph, an attendance heat map and a table of the highest performing employees

sampleAnswers.answer: The visualisations in the data dashboard are easy to read, catering to users of all digital literacy levels. This will positively affect the management team as not all members of the management team will be well versed in understanding data analytics. Hence, by presenting information from the data with visuals that are familiar, simple and have a clean aesthetic and presentation, the entirety of the management team will be able to read and understand what trends and information has been found in the data through the visuals. Because the management team will have a positive user experience when accessing the dashbaord through the visualisations, the team will be able to better understand the trends within their employees productivity. Through colour-coding and simple visuals the team can quickly and easily determine which department has the highest/lowest performance, which months reap the highest/lowest productivity, which department during which months have the highest/lowest employee attendance and which employees are currently performing best. Because the visualisations are dynamic due to the real-time updates of the dashboard, the management team can also track in real-time any changes that occur to employee productivity and then identify what could have caused the change. This will allow the manamgement to understand what factors, such as season, month or attendence patterns, will boost or decrease employee productivity and how they can better manage these factors to achieve higher productivity rates and performance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining that the visuals are 'easy to read' and that 'colour-coding and simple visuals' let the team see which department and months perform best, and how the team can 'track in real-time' changes. The slips such as 'dashbaord' still earned full marks because the ladder rewards the content, so students should not copy them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The data visualisations in the presentation enhance the management team’s user experience by making complex employee productivity data easier to understand. Features like clear graphs and charts allow management to quickly identify productivity trends and comparisons across departments, by tailoring the design to highlight key insights through the use of colour and appropriate graph types. The use of the heat map for staff attendance and punctuality patterns creates a real-time, dynamic representation of department staff absences across the company. The continuous updating, clarity and focus of the visualisations improve the team’s ability to act on the data effectively and in a timely manner.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining the effect on the team: the graphs and charts let management 'quickly identify productivity trends', and the heat map gives a 'real-time, dynamic representation'. 'Continuous updating' and clarity help the team 'act on the data' in a timely way.

sampleAnswers.answer: The line graph of monthly productivity rises from 60 in January to 95 in July, so management can quickly see the peak and the fall after it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining one feature, the monthly productivity line graph, and what it shows about the peak. To reach 3 marks, it must describe how the visualisations as a whole affect the team's user experience or understanding, not just one graph.

sampleAnswers.answer: The dashboard uses graphs and updates in real time, which managers would find useful.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving some relevant information about the dashboard's graphs and real-time updates, without saying how they affect the team. To reach 2 marks it needs to outline one feature and its effect, such as how the productivity line graph shows the trend.

dotPoints.description: Develop and implement criteria for evaluating the effectiveness of user experiences

prompts.question: Identify two criteria that could be used to evaluate the user experience (UX) of a data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a design team has built a new dashboard for a hospital's ward managers and wants to check that it works for them before launch. The team needs criteria it can measure in a usability test.
markerNotes: A criterion must be measurable: name what is evaluated, such as clarity of understanding or time to find information, rather than a general quality such as 'good'.
Two different criteria are needed; 'easy to use' and 'user friendly' are the same criterion.
Briefly say what each criterion measures for the audience, which makes it usable in an evaluation.
commonStudentErrors: Giving visual features such as colour or font as criteria, rather than qualities of the user's experience.
Naming two wordings of one criterion, such as 'easy to use' and 'user friendly'.
Using a vague criterion such as 'it looks good', which cannot be evaluated.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct UX criteria for a data visualisation, each stated with what it measures
1 mark: Identifies ONE relevant UX criterion

sampleAnswers.answer: Two evaluation criteria for the user experience (UX) of a data visualisation are clarity, how easily users understand the information, and efficiency, how quickly they find what they need.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two distinct criteria, clarity and efficiency, each with what it measures for the audience, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: One criterion for evaluating UX is whether the dashboard is easy to use. Another is whether it is user friendly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies ONE criterion, ease of use, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, name a second, distinct criterion, such as audience interpretation.

prompts.question: A company has created a new dashboard for its factory floor managers. Describe how you would evaluate the effectiveness of this dashboard's UX using the criteria of 'efficiency' and 'audience interpretation'.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a manufacturer has built a dashboard showing machine downtime and output for its factory floor managers, who make shift decisions during production. Before rollout, the design team wants to test whether the managers can use it efficiently and interpret its charts as intended.
markerNotes: Describe the method: who the participants are, what task or question they are given, what is measured, and what result would show the dashboard is effective.
Efficiency needs something measurable, such as time to complete a task; audience interpretation needs evidence of what users understand from the charts.
Use the factory-floor context, such as a shift manager finding the line with the most downtime, to make the task realistic.
Answers could include: timed, task-based testing with managers; time to find a figure; open-ended questions or observation
commonStudentErrors: Restating the criteria rather than describing a method, such as saying 'efficiency means fast'.
Proposing to ask managers whether they like the dashboard, which measures preference rather than the criteria.
Describing a general satisfaction survey rather than tasks or questions linked to efficiency and interpretation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes a practical method for each criterion, with a measure, tied to the factory floor
3 marks: Describes a suitable method for both criteria, with a measure or question for each
2 marks: Describes a method for one criterion in some detail, or outlines a general method for both criteria
1 mark: Makes a general statement that the dashboard could be tested with users

sampleAnswers.answer: In usability testing with factory floor managers, I would evaluate efficiency by giving timed tasks on the dashboard, such as finding which line had the most downtime yesterday, and recording the task completion time. Any errors or abandoned tasks would also be recorded, since an abandoned task is evidence that the dashboard is not efficient for a shift manager. To evaluate audience interpretation, I would show a manager a chart and ask open-ended questions, such as what it shows and what action they would take, checking that they read it as the designers intended. These results would indicate whether the dashboard's user experience supports shift decisions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes a timed task with a measure for efficiency, and open questions about a chart for audience interpretation, tied to the managers' shift decisions, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: To check efficiency, I would ask the factory managers to use the dashboard and see how quickly they can do their work. For audience interpretation, I would ask them what the charts mean.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes a basic method for each criterion, which meets the 2-mark row. To reach 3 marks, specify the tasks, the measure and the questions for each criterion.

sampleAnswers.answer: I would test the dashboard with the factory managers to see if it works well for them and whether they like it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement that the dashboard could be tested with managers, which meets the 1-mark row. To reach 2 marks, describe a method for one criterion.

dotPoints.description: Investigate the impact of emerging hardware and software technologies on user interface (UI) and UX design and development

prompts.question: Identify one emerging hardware technology and briefly state how it could change UI design for data visualisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a software company that builds business dashboards is planning its interface for the next five years and is considering which new hardware its users might use to view and interact with data.
markerNotes: The question asks for one technology and a brief statement, so be specific and short: name it, then say what it changes.
The link to UI design is the key point: state the design change, such as charts overlaid onto the real world or gesture control, not only the hardware's features.
Choose a technology that is currently emerging rather than general 'future computers'.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a technology that is already common, such as the smartphone, as emerging hardware.
Naming the technology but not saying how it changes UI design.
Describing a software feature, such as AI prediction, rather than a hardware technology.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies one specific emerging hardware technology, and states how it would change UI design for data visualisation
1 mark: Names an emerging hardware technology with no link to UI design
